title: Rebuilding Life
excerpt: Whatever we send out returns to us in the twinkling of an eye.

inline.s: Louise Hay
author
Life is very simple,
whatever we send out returns to us in the twinkling of an eye.
Do not overlook a single thought, a single word, a single deed,
for they are all creating our future.
I stand within eternal life,
and all is perfect.
The "cause" of all we think and ponder
is creating the "fruit" we shall receive and taste hereafter.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas stand at our left and at our right,
guiding us
to realize the right path that we think, and ponder, and believe.
Most of us
hold mistaken and foolish beliefs,
and cling stubbornly to life.
Why not change ourselves, then,
and make ourselves better and more perfect?
Do not let the past affect us;
the past has already gone by
and is beyond our grasp.
But if we can seize the "present,"
we begin to be free.
If one day we wake up,
repent our former faults,
and dissolve all fear and resentment,
then the supporting power that comes from every direction
will turn our defeat into victory and raise us ever higher, step by step.
It is easy for a person to know his own suffering,
but harder to know the suffering of others.
Yet if you are willing to forgive and hold no grudge,
that is the untying of grievance and the loosening of knots;
the Buddhadharma itself will teach you how to forgive.
The power of wisdom is boundless;
it will bring us the things we want,
if only we act on right guidance.
In my world,
everything is so perfect.

If I were unhappily stranded on a desert island and fated to keep only one readable book, unable to keep any others, I would without hesitation choose this great and monumental work by Louise Hay: Rebuilding Life.

This monumental work not only instructs us as a teacher would, but is written by this woman author out of her own firsthand experience, and so it moves us deeply and carries enormous influence. Every one of us wants to know everything about our own life. This book teaches us how to deal with all of life, and how to make our life sounder and fuller. In it Louise Hay describes the mutual influence between the mind and illness, cites her own personal experience, and gives most penetrating explanations. Thus, simply by reading this book, we can draw on it and learn from it, and handle our lives so that they are both full and happy.
My profession is helping patients with "AIDS"; because of that need I came to know Louise Hay and adopted her various theories and methods for treating illness.

I let every "AIDS" patient listen to Louise Hay’s lecture recording, "Meeting AIDS Positively." After hearing it, the patients received great help; some listened once a day to strengthen their faith, and one patient named Andrew listened once before sleeping and again after rising in the morning.

I observed every patient, and saw that they all became peaceful and full of love because they had listened to Louise Hay’s recordings; and so my admiration for her grew all the more. She truly is a great teacher; with utter sincerity she uses her own firsthand experience, and effectively brings immense help to the patients who need it. One could call her a Guanyin Bodhisattva in this world, saving beings from suffering and distress.
I am honored to see this book published and to write this preface for it. I sincerely hope that everyone will merge what this book teaches into his or her own life.
This book is of great value; and every one of us is of great value too!
To benefit the world and save living beings — such was my motive in writing this book.
I very much hope that everyone can take my firsthand experience
and learn from me to use his own positive strength
to meet the many waves of life.
I once wrote a small book titled Heal Your Own Body, which outlined how the mind causes illness and was well received in medical circles.
After that I received many letters from readers, all hoping that I might produce a fuller work of this kind.
To benefit the world and save living beings — such was my motive in writing this book.

I very much hope that everyone can take my firsthand experience, learn from me to use his own positive strength, and meet the many waves of life. So long as you are willing to put into practice what this book says, you will surely change your bad habits, turn toward the positive side, and advance smoothly.

I suggest that everyone read the whole book through once, and then slowly read it a second time. When you read it the second time, you must carefully attend to the content and carefully understand it. If it is convenient, it is best to study the lessons in the book together with a friend or family member, encouraging one another.

Because each section of the book sets out some particular problem of life and gives your life a positive strength, you should spend an extra day or two on each section until it is familiar, and then put its teachings into practice one by one.
I hope you will trust this book as you trust the Buddha.

At the end of the book I have faithfully told a portion of my autobiography — "My Story." After reading it, each of you will know that however unsatisfactory our past may have been, we all have the power to turn our lives completely around and fill them with upright energy and happiness.
Please be sure to read this book carefully; the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will protect and bless you.
My heart is one with yours!
The life we experience is entirely of our own making.
Every thought we think is creating our future.
The most powerful thing is the "present," not the past, and not the future.
Everyone suffers a great deal because of self-hatred and guilt.
Many people are convinced that they are "not good enough"; you should know that this is only a thought, and thoughts can be changed.
What harms us most is resentment, criticism, and guilt.
If resentment is dissolved, it can even cure cancer.
If we truly love and cherish ourselves, our lives will come to something.
We must give the past a wide berth and forgive everyone.
We must begin to learn to love and cherish ourselves.
Here and now we should accept ourselves and be satisfied with ourselves; and in this way we move toward the positive side.
Every illness in our body is likewise manufactured by ourselves.
We live in an infinitely good world, where everything is perfect; it is only that life is forever changing.
We may say that nothing has yet begun and nothing has yet ended; everything is only experience repeated over and over again. Life never stands still; every moment is fresh.

We are one with the power of the Buddha, and this power enables us to create as our hearts desire. Our own mind can create enterprises of every kind. Every hour and every moment of life is a new beginning, able to break free of all that is old; let us make a wholly new beginning right here in the "present"!
In the Buddha’s world, everything is perfect!
The gate of wisdom stands open at every moment.
Life is very simple: whatever we send out returns to us in the twinkling of an eye.

If we think ourselves good, we become better; if we think ourselves bad, we become worse. All the suffering and all the joy in our lives are entirely of our own making. The "cause" of all we think and ponder is creating the "fruit" we shall receive and taste hereafter. Do not overlook a single thought, a single word, a single deed; all that we think and ponder, all that we say and do, is creating our future.

We must never take the things we ourselves have made and shift the blame onto others, complaining about them; we should know — if there is a fault, the fault lies with us. Our mind cannot be dominated by other people, by other things, or by any power. We should follow the Buddha’s compassionate instruction and fill our lives with peace, justice, and loving-kindness.
People often say the two following sentences. Why not consider which one you yourself also often say?
The two sentences are:
Everyone has ulterior motives toward me and means me no good."
Everyone is a great help to me."
Do not belittle the power of these two different sentences; they will often create different environments for you. Whatever you consistently believe will become fact.

I believe the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas stand at our left and at our right, guiding us to realize the right path that we think, and ponder, and believe. At the same time, our subconscious mind is constantly accepting everything our conscious mind believes. Since what we believe always becomes reality, we should of course choose "Everyone is a great help to me" as our rule of conduct, and should not choose "Everyone has ulterior motives toward me and means me no good" to guide our behavior.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have boundless power and will never abandon us. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas ferry all beings across on the ship of compassion; if we only practice according to their teaching, we can be liberated and at ease, and have whatever our hearts wish.

If you insist on believing that life is lonely and bitter and that no one loves you, then your world may well truly become lonely and bitter and unloved — for you are hiding yourself in a dark place, and the sun naturally cannot reach you. Only when a person can first help himself can the Buddha then help him.

Hurry and let go of every negative thought, and change yourself. If you always believe that love is everywhere — that you love people and people love you — then I believe that so long as you hold firmly to this thought, after a period of time it will surely become fact: you will receive people full of love into your world, and those already within the circle of your life will be all the more full of love toward you; and you, too, will find it very easy to show your love to people.
Most of us hold mistaken and foolish beliefs, and cling stubbornly to life.

I do not want to blame anyone, for truly everyone has already done his best. But if we know that we could live better and could have more understanding, then why not change ourselves and make ourselves better and more perfect? Many people look upon their present circumstances as utterly worthless — what need is there for that? Since this book has come into our hands, it proves that we all need to change ourselves. So please throw away all those foolish thoughts!

Long before we were grown, while we were still small children, we were influenced by every adult around us, and that influence had much to do with our lives. At that time we depended on adults and learned from them how to see ourselves and how to see the world. If the adults living with you were very unhappy, often fearful, guilty, or angry, then you would imperceptibly learn a great deal of this negative attitude toward life and lose your freedom.

Children who have lost their self-confidence often think: "I cannot succeed at anything," "It is entirely my fault," "I am angry, and I am a bad person." Even after we slowly grow to adulthood, we still unconsciously repeat the influence we received as children, and for a time cannot shake it off.

We do not do this on purpose, nor do we deliberately confuse right and wrong; it is only that we carry within an unbreakable "home," and imperceptibly repeat the habits of childhood, unable to break free of the experiences of that time.

Let us calmly consider: we are no longer children now, yet very often we treat other people just as we once treated our own mother or father. At the same time, we often treat ourselves just as our parents treated us in early years, both scolding and cherishing, our manner exactly like theirs. We may angrily say to ourselves again and again, "You never do anything right!" "This is entirely your fault!" and we may also gently say to ourselves again and again, "You did very well!" "I really love you!" Such situations are extremely common, and no one need blame his parents for anything, because our parents were once the same kind of victim; they could not teach us what they did not know.

Some mothers and fathers do not understand how they ought to cherish themselves, and so they do not teach their children how to cherish themselves either. They simply do their utmost to hand on to their children, in slavish imitation, the things they themselves learned as children.

It is not hard to understand our parents; you need only listen to them tell of their childhood experiences, and you will easily know where their fears and their caution came from. Of course, this requires that we be able to understand with a heart of great compassion.

I believe that our relationship with our parents was already destined in a past life. Each of us was destined to be born on this earth at a certain place and a certain time, as the son or daughter of a certain couple. We came into this world because we had many reasons for coming into this world; our sex, nationality, skin color, intelligence or dullness, and all the rest were not formed by chance, and even whether our parents were good or bad and whether our family circumstances were poor or wealthy is the same: we cannot hope that all this, already settled, might be changed to suit our own ideals.

So when we have grown up, we must not complain one-sidedly about our parents — complaining of them in this way and that, even laying all the faults at their feet and thinking that the blame is caused by our parents. In fact, before we were born, we ourselves chose our present parents and were glad to be their children.

Every one of us has a karmic bond with our parents. We depended on them, and as children we followed them with whole heart and mind, learning that whole set of beliefs and institutions of theirs. When we grow up and meet with all kinds of experience, we apply to life the set we learned from our parents, putting it into practice ceaselessly and repeatedly.

Everything we experience comes about according to our former beliefs, former thoughts, and former actions. The words spoken, and all the thoughts held, yesterday, a year ago, twenty years ago, forty years ago, made us what we are today. Yet even so, our greatest power still comes from the "present." For the past has already gone by, and what matters is not the past, but the "present." All the thoughts you hold and the words you speak in the "present" will create your future, creating your tomorrow, next week, next year

If, when you graduated from middle school, you resolved to study medicine and acted on that resolve, then after some years you are a doctor. Let me repeat once more — our greatest power comes from the "present."

You might as well come to know what you are thinking right now — is it positive, or is it negative? Do you hope that your present ideals will become facts in the future and bring some change to your life? Take careful care of your thoughts! At the same time you must understand that our thoughts can often be changed by ourselves. Whatever problem a person runs into, the root of that problem necessarily comes from his thoughts.

Sometimes we hate ourselves, do we not? In fact, this feeling is nothing but a thought making us hate ourselves. The reasoning is obvious: if we often think that we are a bad person, then this thought will manufacture a certain feeling and leave us sunk in that feeling. But if we did not have this thought, then that feeling would not exist. Despondent and absurd thoughts should not be allowed to remain; they should be changed, and once they are changed, the feeling will naturally be very different.

Do not let the past affect us, no matter how negative and painful those past events may have been. The past has already gone by and is beyond our grasp; the life of the "present" is what we need to seize. If we can seize the "present," we begin to be free!

How we think is something we can choose. Although sometimes we habitually repeat a thought over and over, and on the surface it seems there is no room for choice, in fact all of this is our own doing. We have the ability to choose certain thoughts and the ability to refuse certain thoughts. Do you not believe it? Just consider whether we have ever refused to think some positive thought, and it will be clear; then of course we can also refuse some negative thoughts — of this there is no doubt.
I know many people, and among them quite a few are bearing the suffering of self-hatred and guilt and are in urgent need of improvement. For how could a life like that ever become happy?

Many people privately believe that they are "not good enough." We say such things as "I do not do enough" and "I am worthless." If a person always thinks like this, how, one asks, could he have a life full of happiness, health, and love? If a person rejects in his subconscious the idea that he has a good life, how can he go looking for a good life? When a person is always full of self-pity, his abilities weaken, and he easily runs into difficulties everywhere.

In my view, "resentment," "criticism," "guilt," and "fear" are the four very worst habits in our lives. These four bad habits cause enormous problems in our body and mind. They come from our liking to blame others and never daring to take responsibility. If we shoulder all the responsibility, then we will not blame anyone. Even if there really is someone who deserves our criticism, it is entirely we ourselves who drew such a person to our side. When our own inner thoughts are unhealthy and we cannot tell what is right from what is not right, we attract bad people and do wrong things — how can we blame only others for that?

When someone is often criticized, used, and trampled on by others, the same reasoning holds. It is because his inner thoughts are incorrect that he attracts those who criticize him, use him, and trample on him to come and live alongside him. If he can extinguish these incorrect thoughts, those hateful people will no longer come to his side, but will go looking for others to criticize, use, and trample on. Changing our thoughts can change our behavior and influence our future fortunes; if our thoughts are pure and good, good things will naturally come one after another.
Resentment, criticism, guilt, and fear bring illness upon our bodies. Unhappiness brings rheumatism, and long-standing resentment will even bring cancer.

Many patients come to the clinic to see me, telling me of pain here and pain there, and the moment I hear them I know they must have many unhappy matters in their hearts. Some people feel tense all day long, some go bald very early, some develop stomach ulcers, some have a pain in the soles of their feet for no reason at all

These illnesses, in my experience, can be dispelled so long as the patient can dissolve his resentment, and even cancer can be dissolved. This claim sounds rather unreal, but I truly have such experience and such facts.

Not only can every one of us change his attitude toward past events, we urgently need to change it. What was done in the past has already become fact and we can no longer change it, but — we can change our attitude toward past events, and our thoughts about them. Someone once hurt us, and we go on and on using that to make ourselves miserable and to harm our own body and mind — how foolish that is!

I often say to those who harbor resentment toward others: "You should begin right now to dissolve your resentment, for it is not yet too late, and it is still easy. Do not wait until you are about to be operated on by a doctor, or even until you are on the point of death, before beginning — that will be too late. Forgive others! You can do it. If you can forgive others their failings, others can forgive yours!"

If a person wants to dissolve resentment, he must first dispel fear, because when we are afraid it is very hard to gather the thoughts in our mind. So we must first dissolve fear; then, taking all things calmly and unhurriedly, we can naturally produce a power to help us. If we do not change, but only keep thinking of ourselves as a helpless victim and believe that nothing can ever hold hope again, then even the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas cannot resonate with us or help us; we are then harmed by ourselves and fall even further. Conversely, if one day we wake up, repent our former faults, and dissolve all fear and resentment, and if we have right thoughts and right views, then the supporting power that comes from every direction will turn our defeat into victory and raise us ever higher, step by step.
Only by forgiving others can we dissolve unhappy past events.
We must forgive ourselves as well.

We may not know how to forgive others and forgive ourselves; we may not even want forgiveness at all, or may not know that forgiveness is possible. In fact, forgiving others and forgiving ourselves are both necessary. Who is without fault? Even the sages had faults, to say nothing of ordinary people. Forgiveness means giving another person a chance and giving ourselves a chance; "turning weapons of war into jade and silk" is one of all the good things in the world, and it is very important.

Once we know the importance of "forgiveness," we must be able to put it into practice. We can make up our minds and say to a person who once harmed us: "I am ready to forgive you. Though you wronged me in the past, I am determined to forgive you and hold no grudge, and to let you be free and at ease." — This is "dissolving grievance and untying knots." These words carry great weight; you not only set another person free, you set yourself free as well, and will no longer be trapped by resentment.

Many illnesses come from being unable to forgive others. If you want your illness to be quickly cured, then when illness comes you should quickly find out which person in your heart it is that you hate. Once you have found him out, you should forgive him.

If there is someone you find very hard to forgive, that is proof that this is precisely the person you most need to forgive. You need not worry that you do not know how to forgive him; so long as you are willing to forgive, so long as you are ready to forgive, the Dharma itself will teach you how.

It is easy for a person to know his own suffering, but harder to know the suffering of others. Yet once you think it through, you understand that they too have done their very best, and only did wrong against their own will. Since they have done wrong, their suffering is a matter of course, and so is their need to be forgiven.

One thing that matters as much as forgiving others is this — you should love yourself. Though our health may be poor, our money scarce, or our marriage unhappy, all of it is only temporary; as long as we love ourselves, every kind of misfortune will soon pass.

I have found that once a person accepts himself, everything in his life flows naturally. If we can truly love ourselves, our health improves, money comes more easily, our relationships with others improve, and our creative power grows stronger. When all good things come to us naturally, we need not struggle especially for them. To love ourselves and accept everything about ourselves is enough to benefit us beyond measure for a whole lifetime.

Accepting ourselves and loving ourselves creates a sense of security and self-confidence, and so it can bring us sudden inspiration and make everything we do come off easily. Therefore, in the “now,” we should change without the slightest hesitation and at once accept and love ourselves. Once we truly do so, we will surely achieve good results — and those results will not be forced at all, but will come about of themselves, quite naturally.

We should not despise ourselves or think little of ourselves, for that is like putting a lock on ourselves and shutting ourselves inside a lightless cage from which we cannot get out. The only way to open that lock and save ourselves is to love ourselves and accept ourselves, and not to heap criticism on ourselves.

For many years we may have been blaming and criticizing ourselves without letup. That does us not the slightest good; it only leaves us at a loss and not knowing what to do, so why do it? When we accept and love ourselves, all our potential is naturally brought into play, and we do so brilliantly that we astonish even ourselves. If you do not believe it, just think: do you do your work best when someone is standing beside you scolding you, or best when someone is standing beside you encouraging you?
I often feel that in our boundless life everything can be perfect, so long as we act according to right guidance, and the Buddha’s sublime power is beside us every day, helping us.

We must let go of unnecessary attachments and let the Buddha’s knowing and seeing awaken the wisdom within us. Then all the problems we cannot solve will receive clear answers, and every doubt will be resolved at the touch of a blade. All our illnesses will be healed, and we will recover at once, as though a barrier had suddenly fallen away.

The power of wisdom is inexhaustible. It will reveal to us everything we ought to know, and bring us everything we wish to have. When the right time comes, we will lack nothing, and everything will be so beautiful.

blocks.text: Chapter Two: What Is Your Problem?

inline.s: Whenever I ask someone, “What is your problem?” it is quite likely that he will answer me like this:

I am old, and my body is a problem. If it is not pain here, it is pain there, and the pain gives me not a moment’s peace. My eyes cannot see clearly, my ears cannot hear clearly, and every faculty is in decline.”
True enough, these problems really are very common, and I have great sympathy.
Others answer like this:

I never seem to get along with other people. They make endless demands on me, yet they never give me any support. They criticize me and slander me, and there is not a shred of love in them. Whatever happens, they take it out on me; they ignore my difficulties, and they never even give me a chance to explain.”
Yes, these problems really are problems, and I quite agree.
Someone else answers me this way:

I have no money, and what I earn is little and not enough. What I have to pay out is always more than what I earn by hard work, so I can never balance my budget; money alone has left me utterly lost.”
Indeed, when income never covers outgo, that really is a problem.
Others still say this:

I have never once had the chance to do what I like to do, and I do not even know what I ought to do. I have no ability to make others happy, and I always feel there is not enough time; none of my needs and desires can be fulfilled. No one cares about me or helps me live a better life. I am too useless; there is almost nothing I do that turns out right. And I keep putting off the things I ought to do.”
I have indeed met a great many people who set out problems of this kind.

The patients who come to my clinic each have their own problems, and all of them are roughly similar to the few kinds above: either the body is in pain or ill, or they find it hard to get along with people, or else they lack money and are miserable in spirit
, and some even have several of these problems concentrated in one person; it is not so simple as each person having only one.

The patients know they have problems, but they do not know that their problems all come from their thinking, and that it is because their thinking is incorrect that these problems arise. I often ask these patients, “Is your life going well?” “How is your body?”
What kind of work do you do?”
Do you like your work?”
Is your money enough for your needs?”
What is your love life like?”
Have you ever broken up with several lovers? May I know the reason for each breakup?”
Please tell me simply, in a few words, about the surroundings you lived in as a child.”
When my patients answer these questions, I listen carefully to the tone of voice in which they answer, and watch their bodily posture and their facial expressions.

Because thought and speech shape every person’s future, I pay close attention to what they think and what they say. And whenever I have listened carefully to what they say, I can always tell what problems they really have. “To know what is in the heart, listen to what is on the tongue.” When the words a person speaks plainly say one thing but turn it into another, when his tone of voice does not match, when much of what he says does not fit his own experience, then I can be sure: either he is lying, or he has lost touch with his own life.
I also give each of my patients a small notebook and a pen, and have them write five or six sentences on the paper about how they ought to be.
Some find it very hard to write in this way, while others write and cannot bear to stop.
Then I ask them to read aloud to me the sentences they have written. When they read out “I should do such and such,” I ask at once:
Why do you feel you should do that?”
My mother says I should.”
I am afraid it will be bad if I do not.”
Because I have to be perfect.”
Everyone has to do it this way!”
Because I am too lazy, and my height and build do not meet the standard; I am too stupid, too ugly, too useless.”

From these answers of theirs I can see just where their conceptual patterns go wrong. They read, and I only listen quietly, without criticizing. Not until they have finished reading their six “I should” sentences do I talk with them and discuss the word “should.”

I hold that the word “should” is one of the most harmful words there is. When we use the word “should,” we are in fact saying that we ourselves are “wrong”: our past was “wrong,” and our future “will be wrong” too.

We truly do not need to call ourselves “wrong” in this way. We have many choices open to us from the start; things do not have to be one certain way. If I could, I would dearly like to abolish the word “should” forever and turn it into the word “could.” The word “could” shows that we have room to choose, and it also shows that we were never possessed of any such thing as “wrong.”
I ask my patients to make a change: to cross the word “should” off the paper and write in its place the word “could,” and then to read it out accordingly: “I wish I could do such and such
.” In this way, much darkness at once turns into light.
As they finish reading each sentence of what they wish they could do, I ask them:
Then why do you not do it?”
Their answers are plainly different from before:
Because I do not want to.”
I think I would be very afraid.”
I do not know how to go about it.”
I think I am not capable enough.”
In all these answers, the meaning of “wrong” has been deleted.

Very many patients have for years been harshly blaming themselves, criticizing themselves for not having done a certain thing; yet in their hearts they never wanted to do it at all, and it was not in the least to their liking. If they understood that they need not let others order them about, they could set such undone things aside and pay them no more mind, instead of brooding over them; they could be free and easy and thoroughly at their ease.

Some parents think their sons and daughters ought to become doctors or lawyers, and require them to follow their will. If their children have no interest at all in studying medicine or practicing law, then it is quite forgivable that they do not study or practice it well; there is no need at all to apologize to their parents, still less to blame themselves for it.
Whatever self-blame can be cast off with relief may as well be cast off at once; there is no need to wait for another day.

Ever since my patients and I began studying the abolition of the word “should,” they have started to re-examine their lives. At the same time they have discovered that many things they had always hoped to do well did not in fact spring from any real need in their own hearts, but were done only to please others, which is very foolish. Once they awaken to this, the illnesses brought on by mental burden quickly took a turn for the better, because they no longer did things they did not need to do just to please others, and no longer took their failure to reach an ideal as “their own mistake” and torment themselves with it. Thus all pressure vanished, and a new life began from that moment on.

I explain my philosophy to them. I believe life is very simple: whatever we send out will in the twinkling of an eye come back to us in another form. The Buddha’s right knowing and right seeing guide our right thinking and right action, so that we reap what we sow, melons for melons and beans for beans, and receive all the karmic rewards that are our due.

Of course, when we were small children we could learn how to feel about life, how to feel about ourselves, and how to form beliefs only from what grown-ups awakened in us. But whatever we learned as children, once we have grown up we need not put those beliefs back into our lives over and over again. You should know that all our past has passed away in a blur, and what is truly of use to us is the “now.”
We must learn from the Buddha to change ourselves, and we must begin that change in the “now”!
Loving Yourself
However great the problems my patients have, I help them all by the same method, and that method is to teach them to “love themselves.”
Love is the most wondrous and most effective healing power. If every one of us could truly love ourselves, our lives would surely be filled with miracles.

What does it mean to truly love yourself? To truly love yourself you must leave vanity behind and free yourself from arrogance, for vanity and arrogance are the very opposite of the way of loving yourself. Vanity and arrogance are in fact only a kind of fear, whereas loving yourself asks of us a great respect for ourselves, and a deep gratitude for our own life, our own mind, and our own body.

I hold that “love” is a warm appreciation in the heart for oneself, for others, and for life, and at the same time an appreciation of many other different things. In my own case, the things I love with all my heart are:
The many journeys of life
The joy of being able to live in this world
The beauty I see
Another person
Knowledge
The wonder of the mind
Our bodies
Animals, birds, fish
All the plants
The greatness and the mystery of the universe
The Buddha’s support and encouragement
Friends, may I ask what else you could add to this list?
Now let us look into all the ways in which we do not love ourselves:
We constantly blame and criticize ourselves.
We ruin our bodies with improper food, strong liquor, and drugs.
We firmly believe that others do not love us.
We are even afraid of being promoted.
We bring illness and pain upon our own bodies.
We put off the things that are good for us.
We live in confusion and disorder.
We owe people money.
We draw close to people who do not cherish us.
Just think: do you dislike yourself in ways such as these?

I remember one patient of mine who wore contact lenses. One day she and I discovered together a fear from her childhood, a fear that had greatly affected the years that followed, and of which she had been completely unaware. After I explained it to her and guided her through it, the next day she felt uncomfortable wearing her contact lenses. She took them out, and discovered that her eyesight was actually better than it had been with glasses, and that she had no need of glasses at all.

But even so, she still had no confidence at all in her own eyes. All day long she said to herself, “I do not believe it, I really do not believe it, I really do not believe it, I simply cannot believe it.” After thinking this way for a whole day, the next day she put her glasses back on, feeling that she certainly had to wear them and that only with them was she safe. Her behavior proves that when a person has no faith in others, he can even lose trust in himself: her eyes were plainly normal, yet she still would not believe the truth of the facts. In fact, a person’s eyesight is bound up with both his body and his spirit; it is not that it can only get worse and can never get better.
There are also people who feel they are worthless, and that too amounts to not loving themselves.

Tommy was an outstanding artist who often painted murals for wealthy families, yet he himself had no savings at all, and was often so poor that he could not pay his bills. He thought this happened because painting pictures on other people’s walls took so much time that he could not earn much money. In fact everyone knew that Tommy charged too little, and that was why his income was small; those wealthy families would not have refused even if he had asked for more, and might even have felt that the pictures on their walls were all the more valuable. It was only that Tommy thought too little of himself and did not dare ask for a larger fee, so that even hard work could not cover his daily expenses, and he suffered in poverty. A person who does not know how to improve his life but only knows how to make himself miserable is doing himself a great wrong.
There are also people who often feel they are worthless, and at work they tend to feel they have done something wrong, so that their colleagues do not like them.

There are others who, because they went out with someone of the opposite sex once or twice and the other person never asked them out again, believe they must have done something wrong to displease the other, and become terribly dejected. In fact, after two people have met alone together, it is easy for them to find that they are not really suited to each other, and so they do not want to date again. This happens all the time, so why blame yourself?

There are many more whose marriages have failed, who no longer affirm their own worth and regard themselves as eternal failures; this too is wrong. Whether a marriage can last depends entirely on whether the two partners’ temperaments suit each other; there is no question of victory or defeat in it, and no need to think little of yourself.

Some people are even distressed that their figure is not as good-looking as a model’s; some dare not make any decision for themselves for fear of making a mistake; some, to smooth things over and keep the peace, give up their own principles
Just think: do you often feel that you are worthless?
The Perfection of a Baby

When we were still tiny babies, we could be called utterly perfect. A baby does not need to do anything to make itself perfect, because it truly is already perfect. It knows it is the center of the family, and when it has a need it is never afraid to ask or to insist. It conveys its feelings quite naturally. When a baby is unwell, the family is sure to notice, and almost every member of the family, old and young alike, will know of it. And when it is happy, the family is sure to see it, for its smile can make the whole household shine.

A baby is full of love. But if you do not love your baby, then your baby will be listless, and may even pine away and die. Only after growing up can a person learn how to live in an environment without love, but a baby simply cannot do it. Babies love their own bodies, and do not even find their own excrement repulsive; they have immense courage in loving themselves.

Remember, we were all like that once. But when we began to listen to what grown-ups said, and what grown-ups said so often aroused fear in us about everything, we gradually lost the courage we once had and no longer loved ourselves as we had in babyhood.
Mirror Exercise

Sometimes I ask a patient to take a small mirror, look into his own eyes in the mirror, softly call his own name, and say, “I love you, I accept you.” This is a very simple action, yet quite a few patients find it very hard to do. While doing the exercise before the mirror they all seem emotionally unstable; some grow angry, some weep, and some simply refuse to do it. Once a patient even flung the mirror down hard and left the clinic at once, and only many months later did he take up the exercise again.

The mirror exercise may look rather absurd, but in fact it truly helps patients pour out what is in their hearts and lets me understand them quickly. When I discuss their problems with patients who have already done the exercise, it is easier to dig out the heart of the matter. Apart from a few, most patients are afraid to hold a mirror and gaze into their own eyes; that is a psychological sign of being afraid to face reality. I myself had the same experience in earlier days, but later I could face the mirror without any fear, and many patients have been the same. So this mirror exercise is indispensable.
Problems

There was one patient who was extremely concerned about her looks, and especially about the beauty of her teeth. She went to the dentist constantly, one after another, and no matter how many she saw, not one of them could satisfy her. She also went to a plastic surgeon and had her nose changed, and in the end thought herself uglier than before the surgery, and was very dejected. Her problem really was not her looks at all, but her deep conviction that she was inferior to others. With that belief, she naturally felt that everything about her was wrong. This was something her dentists and her plastic surgeon could do nothing about, not because their skill was poor, but because her looks were simply not her real problem.

There was another woman who had bad breath, so foul that no one near her could bear it, and people could only keep their distance from her. She was very diligent, studying and working at the same time, and she strove hard. Her goal was to become a woman pastor. On the surface her spiritual cultivation was lofty, but in her heart she was not only forever competing with others but also full of jealousy and anger, always supposing that others wanted to seize her position, and so she was very hard to get along with. This wrong thinking within her was the cause of her bad breath. In fact she was only frightening herself; there was no one at all trying to take her position. She fixed her attention entirely on dealing with other people and overlooked the fact that it was her improper diet, her poor digestion, and the uncleanness of her mouth and teeth that made others unable to come near her — so that she felt all the more that enemies surrounded her on every side, all of them working against her.

There was also a young man who had contracted a fatal illness at only fifteen. His mother brought him to see me, because the family doctor and the specialists all said he had only three months to live before he must leave this dusty world. His mother was utterly hysterical, and on hearing this became even more frantic, but the boy himself was clear-headed and sharp, and he very much hoped to go on living. He told me he would follow my guidance and do what I asked him to do, including changing his thinking and his words and actions.

His parents had already divorced, and when the two of them happened to get together they did nothing but argue and quarrel, so that he lived in a very discordant environment. And he, for his part, was eager to become an actor and to gain fame and fortune quickly, believing that only with fame and money would people accept him. This notion of his kept him from truly tasting the joy of life.
I taught him to love himself and accept himself, and gave him various methods, all of which he carried out one by one; afterwards his health returned completely to normal.

Now he has grown to manhood and performs the roles he plays at a Broadway theater, fulfilling his dream of becoming an actor. At the same time he can let go of the desire for fame and profit and devote himself single-mindedly to fulfilling his own heart’s wish, and he has truly tasted the joy of life.

Obesity is another illness worth bringing up for discussion; it proves that we often waste a great deal of time dealing with a problem that is not the real problem. Many people spend a great deal of thought and many methods on losing weight, yet in the end remain exactly as they were, with no improvement at all. And so they acquire more problems besides, and they lay every one of those problems at the door of their obesity, complaining endlessly.

In fact their hearts already held other problems, and that is why they became obese. Their real problem is usually that they are too timid and full of fear, and need special protection. When a person has no self-confidence, is afraid, and feels he is “not good enough,” he often becomes very fat. Such people constantly scold themselves and blame themselves for being too fat, and feel guilty with every bite they eat; this is truly a waste of time. If they go on this way, even in another twenty years they will still be just as fat, because they have not faced the real problem within; they have only made themselves more fearful and more lacking in confidence. And after fear and loss of confidence, they gain more weight again, using fat to cover over every fault.

So in dealing with people who are overweight, I never fix my attention on their obesity, nor do I believe that dieting can truly help them. Fat people seldom stay on a diet for long; each time they stop, the obesity returns as before, so dieting is of no use at all. What they truly need, one might say, is to go on a psychological diet — to eliminate negative thoughts one by one.
I always say to people who are overweight, “Let us set the matter of obesity aside for the moment; we must first face some other problems!”

They often say they cannot love themselves because they are too fat. I explain to them that the reason they are fat is precisely that they do not love themselves, and that if they could begin to love and accept themselves, their weight would surely drop. The principle is obvious: when a person can love himself, he naturally protects himself, taking care of his health in every way, not eating too much, not sleeping too much, eating more vegetables and fruit and less rich and greasy food, thinking flexibly and exercising his body. And when a person is full of vitality, his bodily functions are naturally vigorous, so that fat is not stored up to form obesity. For a person to try to lose weight successfully while hating himself is like wanting others to help you while you are unwilling to help others; the goal simply cannot be reached.
I often tell my patients — rebuild your life. This is a most reasonable suggestion, yet some patients actually become angry when they hear it, thinking that I do not understand their real problem.
One woman was deeply depressed, and she said to me, “I came to see you because there is a paper I cannot write and I want your help; I did not come to hear you talk about learning to love myself.”

It is very clear that this woman hated herself deeply and was satisfied with nothing about herself. This self-hatred of hers had seeped into almost every part of her life, including the paper she was writing. So long as she went on hating herself like this, nothing she did would succeed. She had firmly pressed a cap of failure down onto her own head, covering her own ears and eyes.

I urged her to stop hating herself. She would not listen, and left in tears. A year later she came to see me again, still hating herself in the same way, and now carrying many new problems besides; of course, the thesis had still not been written.

It is never easy for a person to change. Take me, for example: I could not manage it until after I had turned forty. I believe that if a person puts forth perseverance, conditions will gather and help will come; but if he keeps casting himself aside, then even the bodhisattvas can do nothing for him.
The Real Problem
I tell others all the time: you must love yourself.

The first thing to remember about loving yourself is not to demand too much of yourself, not to criticize yourself, not to blame yourself. When I ask patients whether they criticize themselves, they always answer me like this:
Of course I criticize myself.”
I criticize myself all the time.”
Others say: “These days I criticize myself less than I used to.”
If I did not criticize myself, how could I ever change?”
One patient said: “Everyone criticizes himself, don’t they?”
I said to this patient: “I am not talking about everyone now; I am asking you, personally. Why do you criticize yourself? What exactly is wrong with you?”

When the patients answered me, I wrote down everything they said. Every one of them disliked something about himself, and what they disliked had a great deal in common. The tall felt too tall, the short felt too short, the thin disliked being too thin, the fat disliked being too fat, those of middling intelligence thought themselves too stupid, the no-longer-young felt too old, the young hated being too young, and those of ordinary looks complained of being too ugly. Some who were really quite beautiful or handsome hated themselves for not being beautiful or handsome enough. Still more said that whatever they did was either too late or too early, and each one criticized himself for being too this or too that. In short, they all loved to use the word “too,” and in the end every one of them would say: “I am not good enough; I am not as good as others.”

And so we finally come to the heart of the problem: they criticize themselves because they feel they are not good enough, not as perfect as others. This is the real, genuine problem, and it is the problem that must be solved. Whether the body is out of order, whether relations with others go badly, whether money is lacking — none of these matters as much as this problem does. For this problem is the root; all the other problems arise from this root. Until this problem is solved, the others can never be solved. When a person casts himself aside, the clever turn stupid, the healthy fall prey to illness, blessings do not come, and the heart loses its spiritual light.
Seek your own blessings” — only those who are full of confidence in themselves can be happy. To be a human being and yet not love oneself: this must never be.

blocks.text: Chapter 3: Where Does It Come From?

inline.s: We have already inquired into this, and we have reached a conclusion: many people feel they are not good enough, not as good as others, and so they are dissatisfied with themselves and do not love themselves. In my own experience, whatever problems people have, they all arise from self-pity and self-abandonment. Now let us look into why these problems arise in them.
How is it that we begin as a perfect, flawless infant, and yet by the time we grow into adults we are full of difficulties, feeling that we have no worth and no love?
Fortunately, most people are not like this. They love themselves and they love others; they accomplish more day by day, and they treasure everything.

A rosebud is very beautiful, and its beauty is kept all along: not only when the bud is in full bloom, but even when the last petal falls. Tender and lovely when the bud is still closed, brilliant and lovely when the flower is open, poignantly lovely as the petals scatter one by one — it keeps its perfection through endless change, and this is truly worth pondering.

We are like the rose as well, changing at every moment, and we too should be perfect and lovely at every moment, keeping the perfection of each stage from infancy to youth, from middle age to old age. Each of us has surely done our best, with our limited knowledge, our limited awareness, and our limited understanding, to steer our life toward what is good; but our knowledge, awareness, and understanding are all insufficient, and so problems constantly arise. Yet if we have faith in the Buddha, we will certainly meet the world with different attitudes and different actions, and reach the state of perfection.
Clearing Out Our Thoughts
Now let us examine our own past and see just what it is that has been directing our beliefs.

Some people think that clearing out their thoughts in this way is bound to be a painful process. In fact there is nothing to fear: before we clear things out and put them in order, we need first to look at them and see clearly just what they are like — exactly as, when you want to tidy a house, you must first look carefully at every single thing in it.

Some things you are full of affection for: you will wipe them over, even polish them carefully, so that they shine more brightly and beautifully. Some things you decide need repair, and you will keep them especially in mind, thinking over how to deal with them. And some things you feel are of no further use to you, so you will want to throw them out — old magazines you have finished reading, old newspapers, used-up ballpoint pens, worn-out shoes and socks; you will drop them into the rubbish bin out of habit.

Since our room is to be cleared out, we should not put it off, for what must be done will be done sooner or later. It is the same when we clear out our thoughts, and our attitude in clearing them should be the same as well. When you discover that some old thought ought to be thrown away, throw it away; there is no need to treasure it, and no need to resent it — just as you scrape the leftover grains of rice off your plate.

Think: would you take food you threw out the day before yesterday out of the rubbish bin and taste it again? Clearing out your thoughts is the same. Surely you would not want thoughts discarded in the rubbish bin to go on directing tomorrow’s life for you. If some thought or belief has long since proved to be of no benefit to you at all, then you may as well throw it out, just as you dump rubbish into the bin. No one has decreed that whatever you once believed you must believe forever, and may never change it. You are perfectly free to break with the old and establish the new, to change everything, and with a brand-new face to reap a brand-new harvest.
Now I would like to use some of my patients as examples, so that we can see where their mistaken beliefs actually came from.
One patient believed of himself: “I am not good enough.”

And where did that “I am not good enough” come from? It came from his father — his father often told him he was stupid. He too hoped to succeed in his career, and his father was once proud of him, because he had ambition, and helped him again and again. Yet he had no confidence in himself, and that lack of confidence filled him with resentment, until in the end he failed in his career again and again. His father supported him time after time, giving him sum after sum of money, hoping to turn defeat into victory, but he could never succeed. The truth is that, deep in his subconscious, because he hated his father for constantly calling him stupid, he unconsciously took revenge on his father through his business failures, making his father lose money.
In the end, of course, the greatest loser was himself. He and his father were never able to dissolve what Buddhism calls the suffering of “not getting what one seeks.”
There was also a female patient who likewise gave rise to problems because of mistaken thinking and a lack of love for herself.
Where did her mistaken thinking come from? It came from her father’s disapproval of her.

She and her father were constantly at odds. She had no wish at all to be like her father in everything; she only hoped that her father would approve of her. But her father not only gave her no approval whatsoever, he criticized her without cease.

There was plainly nothing wrong with her body, yet she ached all over; her father was the same, and when they were together they suffered intensely. She did not understand that the reason she and her father were like this was entirely that each hated the other, that neither loved himself nor loved the other, and so everything was wrong in a hundred ways. She and her father were never able to dissolve what Buddhism calls the suffering of “meeting with what one hates.”
Another patient believed that life is full of danger.

Where did this thought of hers come from? She felt that everything around her was cold and cruel, and that others were all harsh. She could not even laugh, because whenever she happened to laugh she would feel afraid, thinking that something “bad” was about to happen. From childhood she had heard her father warn her again and again: “Do not be too happy, for when you are too happy you will grow careless of everything, and that will give others the chance to harm you.”
She believed her father, lost her joy, and so problems kept arising in her life.
Another patient’s mistake was likewise: “I am not good enough.”
Where did it come from? It came from being abandoned and neglected since childhood.

He was very silent and found it hard to speak, often saying not a single word. For a time he also took drugs and drank heavily, so he could not feel that he was any good. The truth is that his mother died when he was very young, and he was raised by an aunt. This aunt of his mostly said nothing, and when she did open her mouth it was always to scold him.
He grew up in silence; sometimes in the house not a word was spoken for days on end.

Later he had a lover, but this lover of his turned out to be a very silent woman as well, and when the two of them were together they mostly said nothing to each other. He was almost always tasting what Buddhism calls the suffering of “parting from those one loves,” and he was never able to dissolve that suffering.
The Exercise of Negative Instructions

I suggest that people with problems try an experiment: take a fairly large sheet of paper and write out, one by one, all the faults their parents found in them. Then have them spend about half an hour more and write down as well the negative instructions their parents gave them.

What opinions did they have about money? Did they say anything about your body? What opinions did they have about love and personal relationships? What instructions did they give you about your creative gifts? What negative things did they say to you?” I ask them.
After they have finished writing, I ask them to look calmly at the words they have written down, and then to say to themselves: “So many of my own beliefs actually came from my parents.”

I also ask them to take another sheet of paper and inquire still more deeply into many of these questions. I ask them to write down what negative things they heard, when they were small children, from the following people. Those people are:
Family members
Teachers
Friends
People in authority
People in the church
I ask them to fill in this sheet slowly, without the least hurry, taking their time, and to notice what state their own bodies and feelings are in while they write.

The sheets they fill are covered with the negative instructions others gave them. I ask them to wipe these negative instructions completely away from their hearts and minds, to erase them utterly. For all these negative instructions are of no benefit to them; they do nothing but make them think themselves very bad and utterly useless. Positive instructions, of course, are not included.
See the Innocent Child Within You

If we set a three-year-old child in the middle of a room, and then several people together scold him loudly, telling him he is stupid, that whatever he does is wrong, ordering him to do this and ordering him not to do that, scolding him for making the place dirty, and even giving him a few slaps
In this way we would make the child utterly terrified; his likely response would be either to shrink quietly into a corner, or to make the place a worse shambles than before.
This is the result of beating and scolding a small child and not loving him, and it is also why we will never know the gifts and inner potential that lie hidden in that child.

But if we speak to this child kindly, telling him how much we love him, how much we care for him, how we love his looks, love his cleverness, love his abilities, and tell him besides that it is all right to make mistakes when learning to do something, and that whatever happens to him we will stand on his side
Then the potential this child unfolds would surely astonish us greatly!

Every one of us adults is the same: each of us has a three-year-old self hidden inside. If we are constantly scolding the three-year-old within, we will do many things wrong, or shrink back and dare not attempt anything, so that our lives, turn them how we will, never come out right.

If you criticize yourself all the time, it is as though you had a friend who criticized you all the time. Tell me, would you still like him, and work with him happily? To be criticized constantly when one is still a child is a very sad and painful thing. Yet after all, that was a matter of many years ago, not a matter of today. If we still criticize ourselves so mercilessly today, that is what is truly painful!

Look at the words you have written on the paper before you. What is written there is all the negative suggestion you heard as a child. Think: do they match the faults you now believe you have? Are they almost the same?

The answer is very likely yes. For the instructions we received in childhood often influence our whole lives. We were all good children, obediently accepting what the “grown-ups” told us and taking it as truth, as unchanging fact; and because of this, some people cannot help blaming their parents and concluding that they are victims forever. Yet if we do this, it not only wounds our feelings to no purpose, it also fails to solve the problem.
Do Not Blame Your Family

If all we can do is blame our parents or others in the family, that will not solve the problem, because we are still bound up in the problem. Blaming others only drains away our own strength. If we are to break free of the problem, take hold of this present moment, and open up the future, the most important thing is to understand and comprehend everything.

We must understand this: our parents or family members had only limited understanding, limited instructions, and limited awareness. They could only teach us with such limited capacities as they had, and we cannot change the past either. Our present thoughts can shape everything in our future. If we want to break free of the past and be free, we begin from this present moment.

We blame others, in truth, because we do not want to take responsibility ourselves, and so we push the responsibility onto them. This is most unseemly. All those family members who had a negative influence on us, or who once behaved badly toward us, are not beyond forgiveness, for each of them had his own many hardships and many fears, felt helpless before many things, did not know how to cope, and did not know how to treat others rightly. They could only take what others had taught them and teach it to us all over again.

Have you ever thought how much you know about your parents’ lives before they were ten years old? If you still have the chance to ask them, I urge you to ask them and come to know them. When you can know what their childhood circumstances were like, you can understand everything that came later. And once you understand, compassion will arise in you toward them.

If you have no way at all of knowing clearly what your parents’ childhood circumstances were, then you can only use the fragments you do know about them to imagine what kind of childhood they had, and so understand how adults with personalities like your parents’ came to be created.

You need some knowledge, and this knowledge can set your body and mind free. If you do not try to understand and sympathize with your parents, you will never be able to liberate yourself. If a person demands that his parents be perfect in every way, then he will demand the same perfection of himself, and in this way his whole life will be extremely painful. For perfection of every kind is a form of excessive demand, and life should not make such demands.
Choosing Our Parents

Buddhist teaching tells us that our parents are chosen by ourselves, that there is a reason for it, and that they could not but be our parents. If they are good, it is because in a former life we had a wholesome connection with them; if they are not good, it is because in a former life we incurred a debt, and so we receive this karmic retribution. Since we have a connection with our parents, their “weaknesses” are precisely what we must accept; and having accepted them, we can transform and improve them ourselves.

I believe that every one of us is walking the same eternal road. We come into this world not only to “settle karma” but also to learn certain lessons; once these lessons are learned, they will help our progress in this life and the next.

Besides the fact that we are certainly our parents’ children, even our sex, our skin color, and our country are all fixed by destiny. Even if none of this suits us, none of it can now be changed. To have good parents can of course give us a model to follow; and even if they had many faults, that too gives us the chance to learn and improve. Only with parents are we here at all; a human body is hard to obtain, and we ought to be grateful. As for our parents’ faults, once we recognize them we should not repeat them; if we repeat them, then the fault is ours, not our parents’ — for they have already shown us their mistakes by example, which amounts to teaching us.

We come into this world as though entering a school. If you want to become a physician, you go to medical school; if you want to become an auto mechanic, you go to auto repair school; if you want to become a lawyer, you go and study law. Your parents gave you life and raised you; once you are grown, everything is your own responsibility.

Many unsuccessful adults often accuse their parents, saying they should never have brought them into the world; that is as much as to say they want no life and no responsibility. This goes against nature, and it is utterly mistaken.
Listening to What Others Say

It is a fact that people are influenced by others without realizing it. When we were small children, our elder brothers and sisters seemed to us like emperors and empresses, supreme above all; they often made us afraid, and they would say:
If you do that again, I will tell Mother and Father and have them beat you!”
You are too little, so you are not allowed to
You are too stupid; we do not want to play with you anymore!”

Our teachers at school influenced us very greatly as well. Take me, for example: just when I wanted to learn dance in the fifth grade, a teacher told me I was too tall and could never become a dancer; and because I was young, I believed him completely, so that I cast aside all my ambition to learn dance. By the time I came to my senses, my age no longer suited starting to learn dance from the beginning.

People should know that when we are in school, marks and grades are only used to show how much knowledge we have taken in during that period. Yet people often at that very time measure their own worth by whether their marks are high or low, and this too is a very great mistake.

In our early years we all had classmates and friends, and they were as immature as we were. Some classmates would often make fun of other classmates, and it was these classmates who suffered deep and lasting pain.

When I myself was a small child I had this painful experience. Because my name made an unfortunate pun, I was often teased by my classmates, which left me so ashamed that I could not hold up my head — a truly pitiable thing.

Our neighbors too had a certain influence on us. That influence came not only from what they said to us and what criticisms they made, but even more from our own constant worry: “I am afraid the neighbors will think I am too

If we think it over carefully, there are, I fear, other authority figures besides who exercised considerable influence on our childhood. And of course those with the greatest influence include advertising, the media, films, television, and so on. Every time they promote something they use psychological tactics, so that it is very hard for us to escape their lure and very hard not to follow them.

Fortunately we are grown now, and can rise above all the influences we received in our early years. We also know that everyone has the Buddha-nature and that everyone can do very well; so no matter how many negative words we heard in our early years, as long as we are willing to overcome them, we can wipe away all the negative beliefs of the past.
We too once had negative beliefs, and in the end they were overcome.
Truth is the part of us that cannot be changed.”
This question is: “Is it really so?” There are two answers: “Yes” or “No.”
If you believe it is true, then it is true.
If you believe it is not true, then it is not true.

A glass half full of water can be seen at the same time as half “full” or half “empty”; different angles give rise to different views. We can choose among thousands upon thousands of different thoughts, and we have every right to choose.

Most people follow their parents’ way of thinking; but there is no law in the world that says we must go on following our parents’ way of thinking. People should never require everyone’s thoughts to be the same.

Whatever I choose to believe in becomes a fact for me; whatever you choose to believe in becomes a fact for you; whatever he chooses to believe in likewise becomes a fact for him. If your thoughts and beliefs differ from mine, then your life’s course and mine will be entirely different as well.
Study Your Thoughts

If your finances suddenly collapse, that shows that at some level of your thoughts and beliefs you believed you would have no money and would fall into debt and poverty; and so you were sullen and unhappy, and never made any practical plan for stabilizing your finances.

To be sure, good things often do not last; but there is no need at all for pessimism and dejection. Life will not be unfair to you; it is only that you yourself have no fighting spirit, and keep saying: “I can never win, whatever I do.”
This kind of dispirited talk can cloud your own mind and lead you to make wrong decisions.

If you have not yet been able to attract someone of the opposite sex to love you, that too is because you have all along believed: “No one will ever love me,” “I am not worth loving.” Or perhaps you are afraid that someone of the opposite sex will dominate and control you as your parents did. Or perhaps you often think: “People only ever hurt me.” You are the one who first rejects people in your heart, making them not dare to come near you; it is not that everyone rejects you for no reason.

Some people’s health is poor, and they often believe: “No one in my family has been healthy, so my body is certain to be unhealthy too.” Or: “It is because the weather turned bad, so my body turned bad too.” Or again: “I came into this world simply to suffer,” “Troubles never come singly”
They do not look into their poor health and deal with it; they simply accept their poor health with negative beliefs, and of course the body does not get better.

Many people have bad thoughts and beliefs without knowing it. Most people do not know their own thoughts and beliefs; they take everything that happens as natural, like a cookie that is bound to break once it has been bitten.
Whatever the problem, it has its root in thought, and these roots in thought can all be thoroughly changed once one has been reeducated.

Many of the problems that make us suffer and struggle in life feel so real and so difficult, as though they had nothing at all to do with our inner thoughts and beliefs, but were simply things pressing in on us from outside that we can do nothing about. If you think that way, if you imagine that you are a wholly passive player, then you are mistaken.

Buddhism tells us that wherever there is a “cause” there must be a “fruit,” and that the fruit comes from the cause; it does not happen for no reason. We need only think how, in a school, it is always the same few students who are always getting into trouble, and we can see that the school did not force them to get into trouble: it was they themselves who first had wrong causes in their thinking, and these led them to troublesome results. This is a truth very easy to understand.
Look at the problems in your life! Ask yourself: “What wrong thoughts and beliefs of mine have created so many problems?”
Sit quietly, let yourself think carefully, and reflect on the Buddha’s spirit of compassion; then your own inner wisdom will give you the right answer.
Beliefs Learned in Childhood

Some beliefs learned in childhood are positive and beneficial, of help to us throughout our whole lives. For example: "Before crossing the street, look both ways, and do not cross while cars are coming."
and so on.
There are also other beliefs that are useful only when we are small; once we grow up they no longer suit us. For example: "Do not believe what other people say."
and so on. Reaching out to others is something we should no longer fear after adulthood; if we never trust others, a person becomes lonely and isolated, and his development in society is limited.

Boys should not cry" and "Girls should not run and jump" are also beliefs that adults instill in children. Such beliefs often produce men who hide their feelings and women who love to sit still and never move about.

If adults teach a child, "This world is a very cold and heartless place," then the child will take it as truth and believe that everyone in the world is heartless; so he will not dare to associate with others, and will often remain so even when grown.

On the other hand, if adults teach a child, "As long as you are good to others, they will be good to you," then the child’s behavior will be different — as an adult more ready to accept others and to give of his love.

Some adults routinely scold their children: "It’s all your fault!" Scolding of this kind keeps a child perpetually uneasy; whatever happens, he thinks it must be his fault again, so that on reaching adulthood he remains the same, becoming a person who cringes and dares not act.

If a person believed in childhood that he was unimportant, then in every circumstance he will be the one who keeps to the sidelines, even when grown. If his family always ignored him, then when he is an adult he will likewise feel that, amid the crowd, he seems not to exist.

Children in the first grade often have difficulty learning and make their teachers work hard to teach them. So some children, after being blamed by the teacher, come to believe they must be stupid, and plant the banner of stupidity forever in their own hearts.

Some people have very poor childhood environments, which lead them to believe that no one loves them and leave them very lonely as adults. Even if they bring a friend or a love into their lives, these do not last.

Some families give children the belief that "people are never satisfied." Such a belief makes him feel, once grown, that the clothes in his closet are always too few and the money he earns never enough; and he lives perpetually in a state of discontented resentment.
One patient said his family had always believed that nothing turned out well, and felt that things would only grow worse and never better; and so he was himself filled with negative beliefs.

He even hurt his knee while playing ball, and it felt like a great calamity. He went everywhere to see doctors, consulting many different physicians; his knee, he felt, kept getting worse. After a great while, when his knee had fully recovered, he never played ball again. Playing ball had been his favorite sport and pastime, yet he had to give it up — he feared that playing again would bring about something worse.

Another person was influenced from childhood by his father, who taught him, while he was still small, to grab everything ahead of others, or else he would lose the chance and even end up with nothing. So when he grew up he would not help others; even queuing to buy theater tickets, he insisted on pushing ahead of everyone, ignoring all order. Because of this, many people did not want to be his friend, and he suffered great mental distress.

The only way to deal with the negative beliefs learned in childhood is to discard them completely: learn from the Buddha and build a new, positive outlook on life. If you believe in the Buddha, all your problems will be resolved.
We often say: "I am who I am; I have always been this way." We also say: "Things are just like this; they cannot change."
These two statements sound very true, but in fact they are only beliefs, not facts. Yet if we believe them forever, they harden into stubborn facts.

What we ordinarily believe is usually only the opinions of others; but we gather many of those opinions into our own belief system. There these beliefs mingle with our other beliefs and become our own.
Many people, waking in the morning and finding it raining outside, immediately think: "Oh, what terrible weather today!"

In fact, a rainy day is not bad at all; it is simply that the air is damp. If we have proper rain gear, wear suitable shoes, and change our attitude toward rainy days, then a rainy day can become a very pleasant day — at least never worse than any other. Even if you find no poetry in it, you can see that it fills the reservoirs and benefits the grass, trees, and crops; and on rainy days there is less dust in the streets.

But if we persist in believing that a rainy day is a bad day, then every time it rains our hearts sink and we become quite gloomy. We resist the rainy day instead of learning to go along with this present moment.
In truth, the weather is neither "good" nor "bad"; weather is simply weather. But if we regard a rainy day as "bad" and let it affect our mood, then a rainy day truly becomes "bad."

To attain a joyful life, one must first have joyful thoughts; to have a vigorous life, one must first have vigorous thoughts; to have a life brimming with loving-kindness, one must first have thoughts brimming with loving-kindness.
A person’s thoughts lead his actions; sow what "cause," and when the "conditions" ripen, you reap what "fruit."
A New Beginning at Every Moment

I want to tell you again and again: the focus of power is always upon this present moment. Every minute and every second before us can never remain standing still. And so, in this present moment, we can change our minds at once.
Even if we are ill, trapped in negative thoughts, forever hating ourselves, and long beset by financial hardship, it matters not; in this present moment we can begin to change everything at once.
All problems can be wiped away at their root, so that they are no longer a reality of the future; as long as you are willing, you can surely accomplish it.
Remember: in our minds, it is ourselves who do the thinking; in our world, it is ourselves who are the true power!
Our past thoughts and beliefs created all our past experiences.
Our present thoughts and beliefs will create all our encounters in the next moment, the next month, and the next year.
It is not "fate" that guides you; it is "thoughts and beliefs" that guide you.
A monk who had not a penny to his name was able to build a grand temple because he first had the thought and conviction, and then acted upon them, so that finally it became reality.

Dear readers, here I offer you the most precious counsel I have, an honest advice drawn from many years of living. If you do not wish to listen, you may refuse to change and continue to choose your old ways of thinking, keeping all your problems entirely intact.
I say this in all sincerity: in our world, we ourselves are the only power! Whatever thoughts and actions we choose will one by one become the reality of the future!
