If only you begin a new course of action in this present moment, then every instant is a fresh beginning — and this is entirely possible! For friends with problems, this is truly good news!
Friend! Make up your mind and begin your change from this present moment — begin a new life!
Is It Really So?

If you are musing over something, first grasp hold of the thought you have right now. What exactly are you thinking at this very moment? Because your thoughts can truly produce actions in you, consider carefully: do you really want the thought you just had to become a fact?
If your thought is one of anxiety, anger, grief, revenge, or fear, you must be all the more watchful — think it clearly through! Think of what outcomes that unwholesome thought may bring!

Though grasping our thoughts is not so easy — they shift so swiftly, like flashes of lightning — from this moment on we must know what we are thinking. If you find that your thoughts are only negative intentions, cut them off at once and do not let them carry on.
You can change at once, choosing positive thoughts and commanding the negative intentions to depart with firm resolve.

Every guest in a buffet restaurant can face all the food on offer and choose from it what he likes. In the same way, every person who works with his thoughts can choose his own thoughts. And choosing thoughts matters more than choosing food: food is only good-tasting or not, whereas thoughts can shape a person’s whole future course of life.

Therefore, if you choose thoughts that will create problems and suffering for you, that is extremely unwise — even worse than choosing food that upsets your stomach. Of course, unavoidably, we all occasionally make wrong choices; but to err once is enough. Once we know that certain foods disagree with our body, we do not choose them again. In the same way, choosing thoughts must not be an endless string of mistakes; thoughts that create problems and suffering are already too much to entertain even once.

In my early years I met a minister named Charles Polk, who often repeated to us students: "When a problem arises, we should not act upon it at once; instead we should first come to know that problem well."
Our mind can create our future. Therefore, whenever we are dissatisfied with a situation, we must use our mind to change it. Moreover, we must begin changing our mind in this present moment.

For example, you have a good friend. He has always been kind to you, but suddenly the two of you disagree over some matter and there is even a conflict. As a result he wins and you lose, so you seethe with indignation, your mind full of resentful thoughts toward him; you even think of taking revenge on him to vent your anger. Though you also realize that attacking him would only hurt you both and ruin your friendship for good, bringing you no benefit whatsoever, you are still bent on letting off this anger and will not rest until you have had your way

Your mind by now is like a wild horse, charging about in all directions. If you do not immediately rein it in at the cliff’s edge and change at once, then all the friendship between you and your old friend will be destroyed by your actions.

Understand the problem" means to think it clearly through: who is truly right and who is truly wrong? Why did he win and you lose? Now that you have lost, must you take revenge on the winner? Is the thought of preferring mutual ruin a matter of rash impulse, or is it right? Even if your old friend truly erred this time, could you not forgive him for now and wait for him to come to his own realization? Must you behave like a petty person? Why not act like a noble one?
When you at last can change your own mind, the tragedy of a broken friendship will not come about.

In truth, many of the things you believe are against you are not really so. You must use your thought, wisdom, and compassion to understand why others act as they do, and so turn enemies into friends and renew good connections.
If you treat a friend as an enemy, the friend will truly become an enemy.
If you treat an enemy as a friend, the enemy will also truly become a friend.
All dharmas are mind-only" — the Buddha’s teaching is quite correct; your mind determines everything about you.
Deciding to Change
Now, many people raise their hands and surrender in fear to their own worries and problems; most people cling to everything and refuse to attempt change.
Many people will say: "I do not think I can change, and I see no hope of changing, so I do not want to try."

Many others will say: "I think it is better not to change, for I am already used to living in suffering and know how to accept it, even though I do not like suffering. Yet that is still better than going against it, because if I resist it, it may grow worse and become more than I can bear."
In fact, resentment is of no use at all. When something bad happens, we resent it; once the resentment has passed, still other bad things occur, and so we resent again
and in this endless cycle we can never rise above our suffering.
What use is resentment? It is a foolish reaction, a response to life that refuses to understand.
We must earnestly ask ourselves: why is it that so many bad things happen, so that people cannot help feeling resentment?

I believe there must be some belief in your heart that is not right, and that is what gives rise to so much worry and dejection, drawing others to trouble you from time to time. Why do you not change your thoughts and conduct, so as to stop bad things from happening and never need to resent again?

Even if bad things have already happened, you should reflect on the single word the Buddha taught you — forbearance — and meet people with compassion, dealing with problems with compassion. That is the true way to be released from suffering.
As you treat others, so others treat you; if you are generous toward others’ faults, others will also be generous toward you when you go wrong.
If you truly wish to know how stubborn you are, you need only consider whether you are a person who is willing to change, and you will know clearly.

Every one of us hopes to change our life for the better, to handle everything more aptly, more properly, and more easily. Yet, however much we wish it, we often cannot truly change. We would rather have others change to suit us than change ourselves to suit everything.

If you cannot change for your own sake, how can others be expected to change themselves for you? Changing oneself is not easy, yet it is by no means beyond our reach. We need only begin from within ourselves: first change our old ways of thinking, then change the tone with which we speak to others; and spontaneously, the circumstances around us will change as well.

Change your thinking and change how you speak, and you can change your life and make everything better. It sounds easy, yet in practice it is often far from easy, because everyone has his measure of stubbornness — more or less — and also the matter of perseverance — whether he can hold on.

Take me for example: I have always been rather stubborn. Even now, whenever my life calls for a fresh decision and a change, that bit of stubbornness rises from deep within me to the surface, making me resist change and hold on to my old thoughts, so that for a while I become once more an opinionated, resentful, isolated person.
Even someone like me, who has worked at self-improvement for years, is like this — which shows how very hard it is to deal with human stubbornness.

I have made dealing with stubbornness one of my own courses of study and practice it constantly. Whenever stubbornness arises, I never fail to tell myself: I am at an important turning point in my life; I must not indulge in slackness and let stubbornness triumph. Since I have decided to make changes in my life, I must bring about new thoughts and new actions! At that moment I turn deep into my own within, peeling away the layers of old thought one by one, so that each layer of old thought gives way to new thought.

In this process I often meet with difficulty, because some old thoughts are easily peeled away, while others are as stubborn as trying to move a great stone with a feather — the old thought refuses to stir in the least and stands unshaken.

People are often barred from the road to success by serious problems; if they do not overcome them, they will know only failure forever. In replacing the old with the new, the more stubborn an old thought, the more it becomes a stumbling block in life, so it must be removed. Recognize it clearly, confront it earnestly, and with perseverance you will win the victory.

There is one thing we must understand clearly: recognizing that our past thoughts and beliefs were mistaken does not mean that we were not good people in the past. There is no need to grieve and rage over our past; on the contrary, in this present moment of improvement, we should gladly celebrate.
Let us say it earnestly: "I am willing to change."
Say it again and again: "I am willing to change, I am willing to change." When we say this, it is best to place our hand over our chest to show our resolve.

Our chest is a very important center of power in our body; this center can help us put change into practice. By saying and doing this, you acknowledge that you are in the very process of seeking change.
We should know that in our lives there are indeed certain situations that need to be changed. At such a time we should let them change, and not suppress them.

Pay attention to the places where we are unwilling to change, for those are very likely exactly what we most need to change. When you set about it, you will find that the "conditions" that help us succeed are slowly gathering together.
When we say, sincerely and repeatedly, "I am willing to change," our situation truly begins to change.
The Path of Carrying Out Change
We should not only lift ourselves a step higher in thought and intention, but also renew ourselves one by one in other respects.
We should attend to improvement in the spiritual, improvement in the psychological, and above all improvement in the physical.
A true process of healing should give heed to body, mind, and spirit all at once. However, one may begin from any of the three.

Some begin with the psychological, taking courses in psychology or psychotherapy; some begin with the spiritual, learning to sit in meditation and regularly recite the sutras; some begin with the physical, taking up exercise and watching their nutrition.
This is like cleaning our house: it does not matter which room we tackle first, so long as the whole house is cleaned.
If we can advance on all three at once, so much the better. Doing so can shorten the period of physical decline and restore health all the sooner.

An old Chinese proverb says that "illness enters through the mouth," holding that many diseases arise from improper diet; hence there are many prohibitions regarding food. In daily life people value "food tonics," and after illness they not only take medicine but also observe "dietary restraints." These sayings and practices may seem quite "old-fashioned," yet analyzed with a modern mind they are very "scientific" and entirely in accord with the way of health. Indeed, many of people’s illnesses are often caused by improper diet. Common sense tells us that inadequate nutrition certainly undermines health, while excessive nutrition also brings on many diseases. Moreover there is the matter of "food allergy," which has already aroused widespread concern.

In the past, people knew only that seafood such as fish, shrimp, and crab caused food allergies, and that other foods did not. But with the advance of medicine it has been confirmed that the foods capable of causing allergies number well over a hundred kinds. "Food allergy" is not merely a matter of an itching skin; it can be severe enough to cost a person his life. For this reason I do not lightly draw up lists of food nutrition for anyone, unless I know precisely how his "food allergies" stand. Some foods suit certain people but not others; other foods suit still others but not some; each case must be studied in detail, and we cannot treat all alike.

There was a patient who had always been fond of drinking milk. When he later developed a stomach ulcer, he was all the more convinced that he should eat more fluids to improve his condition; so whenever he felt thirsty or slightly hungry, he would use milk to quench his thirst and satisfy his hunger. As a result, though he took the doctor’s medicine, the diarrhea did not improve but gradually grew worse — more violent and more frequent — and he grew thinner day by day. The doctor told him that he must not drink too much milk, but he would not listen, believing that without milk his body would be all the more lacking in nourishment. He stopped the medicine, which had done nothing for his diarrhea, and came to my clinic to see me. I asked him to stop drinking milk entirely from that very day; in only a day or two his severe diarrhea cleared up at once and his body grew sturdy and strong again. For this patient the saying that "illness enters through the mouth" was altogether apt. Examples of the same kind are too many to count.

If a person indiscriminately gives himself "nutrition," bad consequences often follow; so one cannot be too careful. Yet ordinary food is not so frightening as to make everyone ill. The main matter is whether the person who eats it does so appropriately. If the amount eaten is not excessive, there is certainly no great danger; on this point you may set your mind at rest.

My own view on nutrition is very simple: as long as each day you eat many foods of different colors, that is enough. If a certain food always leaves you feeling unwell after eating it, you need to give it special attention; once it has been confirmed and proved again and again to be bad for you, make up your mind never to eat it again.

If you are a parent with young children, you must all the more take your children’s diet into account and observe it carefully. In general, meat carries the most toxins; even if you are not allergic to it, you should not eat too great a quantity. It is best to replace it with protein-rich legumes from the plant kingdom. This also explains why so many more people are becoming vegetarian now — that is the very reason. The pity is that many are accustomed to eating meat, and to give it up all at once is not easy for them; in such a case we let things take their natural course and go slowly. I believe that once people’s ideas change, they will gradually put it into practice.

There are also many Westerners who, after eating a vegetarian diet for a while, find themselves becoming anemic and so have to return to eating meat. This is because in their markets the variety of vegetarian foods is too limited, so they cannot take in complete nutrition. I believe such situations will change with need in the future: as long as food merchants put their minds to it, things will be different.
No matter in what area a person changes, there will be a day or two when the body feels unwell — whether it is a change of diet, a change of one’s system of thought, or beginning to sit in meditation

it is all the same. It may even seem much worse than before the change. This is a necessary phenomenon of the old giving way to the new, like preparing to scrub a cooking pot that has long been scorched and is hard to clean. We put hot water and detergent into the pot and let it soak, and only then begin to scour it; and at that moment the pot truly becomes a mess, looking even worse than before we set about cleaning it.
But if you keep on scouring, before very long you will have a pot that seems brand new.
It is the same with tidying up one’s mental system.

When we steep ourselves in new intentions and thoughts, all our former turbid thoughts rise to the surface for you to witness. But as long as you keep building new, wholesome thoughts, before very long you will have an entirely new system of thought, no longer disordered and unwholesome as before — truly making everything about you fresh and new.

For our own good we all wish to change what is bad in our lives; whatever the method, so long as it helps us, we should accept it. Here is one method — many people have used it, and I have used it myself. The method is this: tell yourself that you are willing to change.
Stand before the mirror and tell yourself: "I am willing to change."
Doing this gives rise to great power, because you have declared your resolve. But if you feel hesitant, or are simply unwilling to change, then ask yourself why it should be so.
What old belief is it that you are still clinging to?
Please do not blame yourself; simply notice what it really is, and that is enough.
Whatever that belief may be, I can assure you that it is certainly bringing you a great deal of trouble now, and will bring you still more in the future.
Do you know where it came from?

Whether you know or not does not really matter. What matters is that we must take some action to dissolve it and clear it away. Look once more at yourself in the mirror — look deeply, gaze into your own eyes, summon your courage again, and say aloud: “I will dissolve all resistance!”

This is very important, because when we were small children the grown-ups at home would often open their eyes wide, look at us, and tell us not to do this and not to do that. We obeyed, and many of our negative beliefs came to us in just this way.
Even now, whenever we look into a mirror, thoughts arise and we criticize our own appearance, linking it to one shortcoming or another of ours.

To change, we must still stand before the mirror and look into our own eyes — but this time we should speak positive, encouraging words to lift ourselves up. This is very effective, and good results come quickly.
I myself am a witness: it changed me, and I have benefited from it.
The rhythm of life is flowing, is changing."
We often carry very deep old thoughts and old beliefs hidden within us; we must pay attention to them, take notice of them. Only by paying attention and taking notice can we change them.

Pay attention when you feel grieved or resentful; take notice when your situation is not good. Those are extremely important moments, for they mean that the old thoughts and beliefs are no longer lurking deep within; they have surfaced.

If at this important moment we pay attention and take notice, we will draw near to a good teacher, a helpful friend, or we will seek out certain books and gain certain knowledge; that will show us new methods and a new road, enabling us to deal with and dissolve our long-standing bad thoughts and bad beliefs.

My own awakening came through a friend of mine. He told me of a gathering I could attend; when I heard about it, something within me responded, and so I went alone. Small as that gathering was, it turned out to be the first step on my road to wholeness. When I think of it now, that gathering influenced me enormously.

When people take their first step, they often feel that it has begun rather foolishly, that it makes no sense, or else that it is too easy. Their minds will not readily accept it, so that they do not want to follow it; their resistance is very strong, and even the thought of it arouses aversion.

Such a reaction is quite normal. But we must understand this: since we already have the intention to change, this first step is a very important first step, the first step we ought to take; it can change us, help us, and carry us to the fulfillment of everything we hope for.

Impatience is a form of resistance. What we resist is learning and changing; we want to reach the sky in a single step, to get the thing done and finished all at once. If that is how we are, it shows that we have not given proper time to learning how to dissolve our problems.

If you want to go from this room to another room, you must first rise from your chair and walk step by step in the direction of that other room before you can arrive there. To sit in the chair saying you want to go to the other room while never moving yourself is useless.

The same is true when difficulties arise in our lives. If we want to solve them and yet never begin to work on them, they naturally cannot be solved. One must walk step by step; one must not be impatient, for impatience never accomplishes anything.
We should take responsibility for the problems we ourselves create — this understanding is also very important.

I am not saying that you should feel guilty, or that you should regard yourself as a villain. I want you to recognize the power within you, a power that can turn everything: it can transform your thoughts, and it can transform the course of your life, turning you from suffering toward blessing. This is what the Buddha solemnly taught us.

In the past we unwittingly used our own power to create the experiences that caused us pain; we did not even know what we were doing. Now we must recognize our responsibility and begin to pay attention and to learn how to use our own power to create and to welcome a future that is positive and full of good deeds and good fruits.

Many patients come to me asking for help with their problems, and I show them how to look at a matter from a new angle, how to forgive someone and hold no grudge. I have noticed that as I speak, their lips are often tightly closed, their arms folded across their waist and belly, and their fists even clenched.
From these postures I can see that their resistance is extremely strong, but I know that those very words are exactly what they most need to heed.
All of us have lessons to learn. The hardest lessons must be the ones we most need to choose; if they were quite easy, there would be no need to learn them at all, for we would already understand.
Attend to the lesson you need to learn
If you understand that everything you resist most is exactly what you most need to accept, then you can face your greatest present problem and change it.

You should let go of attachment, give up resistance, and let yourself learn the lesson you need to learn. Once you have done so, the road you travel will be easier to walk from then on. Never let your resistance block your progress and put an end to your changing.
We can begin the work of change on two levels: first, see your own resistance clearly; second, go on changing your thoughts.
The following behaviors are expressions of resistance:
When a serious problem comes up in conversation, we suddenly change the subject.
Or we leave that place and are no longer with the others.
Or we deliberately slip away into the restroom.
We often arrive late on purpose for appointments.
We plead illness in order to avoid seeing people.
We deliberately keep busy with work and ignore people.
We waste time and avoid touching what we ought to face.
Our eyes look elsewhere instead of where they should be looking.
We avoid thinking and idly leaf through magazines.
Whatever we do, we refuse to put our heart into it.
We spend a great deal of time eating and smoking.
We invent reasons to stop associating with people.
Whether on purpose or not, we break things at home.
Besides all these situations, we sometimes resist with words as well, saying again and again:
It is no use."
My family would never understand."
If I am going to change, I may as well change the whole person — I had better change my name too."
Only crazy people need psychotherapy. Psychotherapy is a game movie stars play."
No one can help me with my problems."
People do not understand why I am always worrying or getting angry."
My situation is different from other people’s."
I do not want to trouble anyone."
Things will work themselves out."
The reason I do not do it is that no one else does it."

Besides often showing themselves in the behaviors and words above, a person’s resistance also shows itself in rigid opinions. Such opinions are generally picked up from other people and then applied to oneself at random. They are:

Moreover, we often look for reasons in other people, resisting everything with a ready supply of excuses. We say:

Procrastination and evasion are also expressions of resistance:
I will do it a little later; there is no hurry now."
I do not have enough energy just now."
I have no time right now."
Taking so much time out would interfere with my work."
That is a good idea; let me consider it slowly."
I have too many other things to do."
I will think about it again tomorrow."
Let us wait until I have finished what I have to do."
Now is not the time."
It is already too late."
Refusing to admit that one needs to change is also a form of resistance:
There is nothing wrong with me."
Nothing I do will solve the problem."
I have always been like this; it is no big deal."
What good would changing do?"
As long as I ignore the problem, it will take care of itself."
The greatest resistance of all is fear — fear of everything unfamiliar, fear of this, fear of that:
I am not ready to change yet."
I might fail."
They might refuse my request."
I wonder what my neighbors would think?"
I do not like telling anyone my private troubles.’
I dare not tell my family.’
I do not know enough.’
I might get hurt.’
I do not want to change.’
I should not spend money on a doctor.’
I would rather die than see a psychiatrist.’
I do not want anyone to know I have a problem.’
I dare not express my feelings.’
I do not want to talk about my problems.’
I have no energy to do it.’
If I did, who knows what the consequences would be.’
I am afraid I would lose my self-respect.’
It is too difficult.’
It might cost me my friends.’
I do not trust anybody.’
My profession brings me into contact with many troubled people, and I have grown used to hearing them use the words above to express their unwillingness to change.
One day a woman came to my clinic far later than the hour she had agreed upon. She complained of pain all over her body. An accident had injured her back, her neck, and her knees.

While she was telling me this she was quite unable to speak of it clearly; but the moment I said, “Let me talk with you a little,” she at once became restless, moving from one chair to another, then wanting to go to the bathroom, then wanting to make a telephone call, so that I could never get anywhere in discussing her problem.

In the end she said that her elder sister and her mother, too, had each injured their backs twice in accidents, and that none of them had ever discussed their problems with anyone, so she did not want to discuss hers either.
In truth she suffered not only from bodily pain; her resistance was very strong as well.

Another patient who came to me for help told me that he himself was very shrewd, that he knew how to speculate and could make a great deal of money. Yet he was also desperately poor, often unable to pay his rent, and at times he had not even the money to have a telephone installed.
I asked him to break off his bad habit and stop speculating. He insisted that unless something good happened in his life, he could change; otherwise he could not.

When a person has both the bad habit of speculating and no skill in using money well, how could anything good ever appear in his life? To resist change with an excuse like that is nothing but deceiving oneself and deceiving others.
There are people who never change themselves, but do nothing day and night but demand that their friends change. This is plainly another form of resistance. For example:

A man came to my place, and only after we had talked did he learn that I am a psychotherapist who uses no drugs. He was astonished. For a friend had told him to come and see me, and the friend had even paid the fee for this visit; yet he himself believed that he had no psychological problem at all.
There was another man who asked me to go to his friend’s place to treat his friend. I went, only to discover that his friend knew nothing about the matter; he had no such need at all.

When we come upon a good book, a good play, a place of beautiful scenery, or some delicious thing to eat, we often want to share it with our friends. But when we ourselves need to change, we cannot force others to change. To change ourselves is already a very difficult thing; how then can we demand that others change? Especially when others have no intention whatever of changing, it is even more impossible. If we insist on doing so, we do nothing but wound the friendship between us.
I, too, help only those who come to me for help. I never ask my own friends to change.
We often do the same thing until it becomes a habit and turns into a need.

Such needs come from our beliefs. Needs can be divided into two kinds: one kind is positive, the other negative. Because we have faith in the Buddha we recite the Buddha’s name; because we recite the Buddha’s name we gain samādhi and wisdom; and so our habit of reciting the Buddha’s name is a good habit. The need to recite the Buddha’s name belongs to the positive.
We rise early every day, do our morning exercises, and breathe fresh air until this becomes a need, a habit; and this habit and need bring us vitality and health. It too is positive.
On the contrary, the daily needs and habits of some people belong to the negative. For example: eating fatty meat every day, smoking every day, squandering money every day, drinking every day

and even needing abnormal relations with the opposite sex, needing to scold people, needing to keep company with bad friends; some go further still, until they even need to commit crimes, being accustomed to doing dangerous and immoral things at every hour

They may already have said to themselves many times over, ‘I will never do that again!’ Yet no sooner are the words out of their mouths than they go off to smoke again, to drink again, to do things that wrong themselves and wrong others.
Though they have also blamed themselves again and again: ‘Not a shred of willpower! Not a shred of desire to improve! This is really too disgraceful!’
What use is that? It does nothing but add to the burden of guilt they already carry, and they remain exactly as they were.

Whatever problems have arisen in their lives and need to be solved, those problems are only a surface symptom, an outward show of a result. To want to remove the symptom without laying hold of the place from which the symptom springs, without seeking out the root of the problem, is useless.

Most people believe that if only the person with the problem makes good use of his willpower to deal with his own problem, he may well succeed. To think so is far too naive! If at some moment he relaxes his willpower, will not his problem appear all over again?
Willpower without roots cannot stand firm.
The Willingness to Let Go

I say to my patients: ‘You must have some unwholesome habit and need, or you would not find yourself in your present situation; if you had none, it would not be so. Let us work together and think of a way to deal with it. The first step is that you must be willing to let go of the unwholesome habits and needs. When you are certain that there is no need to do those things, you will naturally no longer want to smoke, no longer want to eat too much rich food, no longer want to take up with bad friends — all those things that harm you.’
The maxim that benefits people is this: ‘I am willing to let go, to let go of unwholesome needs.’

Anyone with a difficult problem can use this maxim. Since you are willing to let go, you must go on thinking from there: what is it that you are willing to let go of? A person with a bad habit knows very well what it is; since in principle you are willing to let go, you cannot go on committing that same mistake.
But if you resist even the maxim above, then you will indeed find it very hard to improve. This maxim, in any case, is one you ought to follow.

Let me remind everyone once again: to turn weakness into strength, defeat into victory, there is only one greatest secret — to be willing to let go of your past bad habits. You must first tell yourself: ‘I am willing to let go!’ In Buddhist terms this is ‘breaking attachment.’ Attachment is not good; all unwholesome attachment must be broken.

People often spin cobwebs all around themselves; these cobwebs block a person’s progress, so the first thing to do is to destroy the cobwebs. Have you ever had the experience of untangling a snarled skein of thread by hand? If you have, you surely know that if you pull at the thread wildly, you will only make the tangle harder to undo. You must undo that ball of thread very carefully and very patiently, or you will make it worse and worse. It is the same with untying the knots in your mind: if you want to untie the knots in your mind, you must undo them very patiently, and it is best to ask an expert for help. And most important of all, you must keep cheerful and full of confidence throughout the whole process of untying.

As long as we have confidence in ourselves, we will create the future we envision. To look only at the outward signs and pay no heed to the beliefs within, is not to prescribe the right medicine for the illness; only by uncovering the cause of the illness will we stop wasting our energy to no purpose at all.
Every kind of illness we have, whether it be mental or physical, has a source; and this is what we must attend to closely.

Some patients believe that they ‘have no value in living’; they will not go to a doctor even when they are ill, but put it off day after day, delaying again and again. In their subconscious there is a longing for death, and this is the root of their illness. If this root is not removed, then even without illness they will make themselves ill; a small illness will drag on until it becomes a serious one, and they plant the seed of disaster for themselves.

If a doctor only treats the head when the head aches and the foot when the foot aches, that is certainly no way to help such a person. It is like a plant whose root has gone wrong: you want to save it, yet you work only on its branches and leaves — what use is that!
In Fact, Anyone Can Succeed

I had a student who was a great failure in life, yet he loved to have everyone’s attention. So every time he attended class he had to arrive late, and by arriving late he made everyone focus their attention on him.

The reason was that at home he was the youngest, and in everything his elder brothers and sisters went first. From childhood he had watched his elder brothers and sisters take the things they needed first, and he was always the very last to get anything. Waiting on the sidelines and longing became a habit with him. To this day he has never once thought that he might have an advantage over others, so he simply withdraws and does not strive; and whenever others succeed, he does not celebrate with them, never shares in their joy. He will pity himself:
Why can they get it, while I never can?’

He does not develop his own talents; he only envies the success of others. Day by day he feels himself more and more worthless, until he lives in dejection and depression, not in the least like a young man in the very prime of life for vigorous endeavor.
The opposite of him is another of my patients. She was a woman already seventy-nine years old.

In former years she had always made her living by teaching students to sing, and many of her students appeared one after another on television and became advertising stars. She told me that she too hoped to appear on television and become an advertising star like those students of hers; but because of her age she dared not think of it and dared not try, deeply afraid that she would only fail and never succeed.

I was very glad she had this aspiration, and I told her: ‘If you want to do it, why not give it a try? I think you would find television advertising interesting; there are many businessmen out there looking for people like you to advertise for them. You can step forward and sound out their intentions; very likely you too can become an advertising star on television!’

When she heard my words she took courage. She made many telephone calls and got in touch with those concerned, saying to them on the phone: ‘I am a very old woman, and I would like to do some television advertising.’

Not long afterward the opportunity came, just as she had hoped. Her commercial went on television. And with that one appearance she became an overnight sensation; from then on she never stopped this work, and she truly became a television advertising star.
I often see her on television, and many magazines carry her photographs.
However old you may be, you can still achieve something new; and the more interest you take in what you do, the greater your chance of success.
Conversely, if a person always withdraws and lacks confidence, then even if she is young she will not succeed.
Do Not Overdo Self-Criticism

Self-criticism does not change our procrastination and laziness. We should not use our strength to criticize ourselves, instead of using it to free ourselves from old habits of thought and to cultivate new ones.

We should hold this belief: ‘I am willing to let go of the old thought that says “I am worthless.” In this world, so long as I do good, I will naturally receive all good things. I love myself, cherish myself, and accept change; causes and conditions will help me accomplish all that I aspire to.’

Please tell yourself: ‘I will spend however many days it takes to make these beliefs real. By thinking unceasingly of the compassion of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, my procrastination and my other bad habits will surely grow less day by day.’

From within my own heart I will uncover my Buddha-nature and be selfish and despondent no more; I will set my system of thought in order, casting out what is old and bad, and bringing my own strengths to the fore.’
If you truly repeat the beliefs above again and again, they will certainly help you change your life; cast off unwholesome old thoughts, and your circumstances will naturally improve day by day.
Plant good causes and you reap good fruits.’ This law is known to all, and understood by all.

Why waste more time and spirit holding yourself to be utterly worthless? Even if we have done wrong, it is only because there are incorrect thoughts in our thinking; it is those incorrect thoughts that make us do incorrect things. So once we change our basic thoughts and intentions, we will never be that way again.
Everyone must clearly recognize this: your problems all come from your thinking. Still, you may set your mind at ease, for thinking can be changed.
Learning the Buddhadharma is one of the best ways to improve one’s thinking’ — this is what I propose to everyone.

Buddhist teaching tells us that nothing in the world is unchanging: what is good can of course turn bad, and what is bad can also turn good. Having learned the Dharma, one can both improve and need not fear falling; casting off the anxious mind that frets over gain and loss, one reflects that all things in this world are ultimately empty — what is there to be so tense about?

So long as a person is open and at ease, not anxiously seeking fame and profit, and with the practice of ‘precepts,’ ‘samādhi,’ and ‘wisdom’ devotes his whole heart to good, he will naturally live better day by day and grow healthier day by day, able to enjoy this life to the full and to pave a broad, level highway for the next life as well.

We need not worry about our own success or failure, lest the more we think the more muddled we become; we need only hold others up as a mirror. For the success and failure of others are worth our deep reflection and can inspire us. How many people have summoned the wind and called the rain, their power shaking all directions — and what became of them in the end?
How many people have been triumphant in love, beside themselves with joy — and what became of them in the end?
How many people have been healthy as an ox, looking about them full of pride — and what became of them in the end?
The more a person possesses, the more he loses; why envy others?

The Buddha gave up the glory and wealth of a prince, practiced austerities and saved others, and with his bare hands attained the great accomplishment; he is our best example. If we can learn from the Buddha, our lives too will be made utterly new!
Be Kind to Others and to Yourself

I have a patient who, whenever she is unhappy, does not face the problem that makes her unhappy; she only eats and eats and eats. But after eating she hates herself, hating herself for eating so much again and making herself so uncontrollably fat!

She had a history of loving to eat, and it was her parents who encouraged it. When she was still a small child she often ate the food left over by others — sweet or salty, main course or snack — she could always eat it, at any hour. When her parents saw this they praised her good appetite and sincerely delighted that she ate so much and grew so plump; before other people they were very proud.

And so, from childhood to adulthood, she formed the habit of eating heavily, until at last she grew so fat that it was hard for her even to walk one extra step. Although she now knows that she does not need to eat so much and must not eat so much, the long-accumulated habit is hard to change. Her problem and her heavy eating have formed a vicious cycle.

A three-year-old child has limited understanding; whatever his parents teach him, whether negative or positive, he accepts completely, taking all of it to be correct. A person’s later experience unfolds according to what he was taught at the age of three; and just as his parents treated him at three, so will he treat his own children in the future, and even treat his grown-up self in the same way.

When people blame themselves, it is as if they were treating themselves as a three-year-old child. In truth, to blame a three-year-old child is already wrong; how much more so when one is not a child at all! Adults should treat children with kindness, and one should treat oneself with kindness too.

Proper remorse is a good thing; blaming oneself and hating oneself is not. Some people, having developed a fearful heart in childhood, remain afraid of this and afraid of that even when grown, careful and trembling all day long. In such a case, if they blame and hate themselves, it does no good at all. Just think: if a small child stood before you and felt very frightened, how would you treat him? Would you be angry with him? Or would you hold out both hands to comfort him and give him a sense of security?

Perhaps when you were small, the grown-ups in your household were too busy and had too little time, and did not know how to comfort you well. But now you have grown up and should know how to do it; how can you then go on neglecting that three-year-old child, not comforting him, not giving him a sense of security? Is that not too heartless, too hurtful? And besides, that three-year-old child is you, here and now!
What happened in the past has become the past. Now you should treat yourself well, for if you do not treat yourself well, others will not treat you well either.
What a frightened child needs is not blame but comfort. Blaming yourself only makes you lose still more confidence and feel all the more that there is no way out anywhere.
Our inner heart is at times indeed very like a small child; and when this small child feels that everything around it is unsafe, it will bring us a great deal of trouble.

Every small child is afraid of being disliked by others; the feeling of being looked down on is very hard to bear. And every grown man or woman is likewise afraid of being looked down on and blamed by others.

Please be full of kindness toward yourself, as toward a small child! A child needs love and needs the appreciation of others; so do you. Only after you have received love and appreciation can you develop your highest potential.
All sentient beings have the Buddha-nature.’ The Buddha appreciates you; you too should learn from the Buddha and appreciate others, and appreciate yourself.

The most useful teaching in the world is one that can show a person how to change himself. If it cannot do that, then it is a useless teaching. I very much like to be guided, because I am a practical person: while I live, I want to live a little better. If a teaching cannot convince me, then for me it is completely useless and I will not accept it. In their basic needs, the thing people most hope to be guided in is this:
) To cultivate the ability that makes us willing to let go of old thoughts and give up bad habits.
) To control one’s own mind, keeping what is good and casting out what is bad.
) To be able to forgive oneself and forgive others, to save oneself and save others.

These three seem very hard to accomplish, but in fact they are not. If a person can follow the Buddha’s guidance and truly put it into practice, they can certainly be done. Even if matters do not go smoothly, after a period of difficult struggle the effects will inevitably appear clearly.

Of course, in this world there are still many regions and many people who have no opportunity to hear the Buddhadharma and must feel their own way along; their difficulties will be somewhat greater. When they try to give up some old habits, the whole situation often looks particularly bad. In fact this does not mean the change is going badly; it is only that at the beginning of change the situation always looks worse, because the stains that were hidden come floating up to the surface for you to see.

To be able to change is always better than not to change. If we are only willing to begin, sooner or later it will take effect. We must never stop just because of a small setback; we must keep pressing on.
Now let me give a few real examples, to see what happened to other people. The following are all words I heard with my own ears:
I am changing, hoping to make my finances prosper; and to my surprise I went and lost money twice in a row.’
I am changing, hoping to make my body healthy; and to my surprise in the space of one month I caught two bad colds.’
I am changing, hoping to show my ability in my work; and to my surprise I suddenly lost the job I had.’
I am changing, and I have begun to give up smoking; and to my surprise, while I was giving up smoking, I quarreled with my best friend.’

The problems these people met with in the course of change really had no direct connection with their changing. There is no need at all for them to feel discouraged because of it. Since the change has begun, they must persist to the end; only by persisting to the end can one ‘wait for the clouds to part and see the bright moon.’

Success is not to be reached by standing still in place, nor is it to be had for the mere taking the moment one sets out. The road is often anything but broad and level. Since you have resolved to improve your finances, what does it matter if you lose money twice in a row? Failure is the mother of success: once you have worked out the causes of those two losses, you will not repeat the same mistake; and your chances of turning loss into profit greatly increase. Keep working at it, and the goal of prosperity will certainly be reached.

Quarreled with your girlfriend? No problem. A quarrel can actually help each to know the other; it is no bad thing, still less is it fatal to love. If after a big quarrel the knot of the problem is untied, the relationship between the two will take a step forward; it all depends on whether both are truly sincere and whether their communication runs into trouble. If there is both sincerity and communication, then the flower of love will surely bloom.

It is so between man and woman, and so between friends. Quarreling and giving up smoking, I believe, have no connection whatever; so long as friends are sincere, even after a falling out they will make it up again, and may even know the value of that friendship better than before the quarrel.

As for suddenly losing one’s job and catching two bad colds in a row, I think these too have nothing to do with changing oneself. When a company lays people off, it is because it has reasons that leave it no choice; and a bad cold is entirely a matter of one’s own weak resistance and infection by a virus. All of that is mere coincidence in time.

In short, change is necessary. A person’s surroundings are changing at every moment, and a person’s own functions are changing at every instant. You cling to the present state and want not the slightest change — how could that be possible? If a person will not adapt to life, life will sink low and go down to the very bottom.

In fact, every one of us is changing; there is not one who is not changing, and all who are alive are striving to change. It is only that some people change as soon as they feel something is slightly wrong, while others wait until matters have gone badly before they change.

When a machine needs oil, to oil it at once is naturally far less trouble than to take it apart and repair it after it has broken down. When using a machine, it is best to oil and maintain it in good time; if you only repair it after it breaks down, it takes more time, more energy, and more money before it can be used again. But if you let it alone and pay it no attention at all, then the machine will only become a pile of scrap metal, of no use to you whatever.

Think of the machine, think of yourself: have you ever oiled the machine? Have you ever repaired the machine? Have you ever, for your own sake, cast out the bad and kept the good, and sought to improve? When you have ‘made certain’ that you need to change, the first thing to do is to ‘put the change into practice.’

How do we put change into practice? First think: in your life, which one thing is most urgently in need of change? Once you have thought of it, you may go and stand before a mirror, look at yourself in the mirror, and quietly tell yourself: ‘I now know that all the circumstances that dissatisfy me are made by myself, and so I must change; I will change all my bad thoughts and bad ways of doing things.’

Of course, you need not face a mirror; you can tell yourself this inwardly, once, twice, countless times. Once you have the awareness of change, the method above can awaken your subconscious. The power of the subconscious is several times greater than that of the conscious mind; when the two work together, they can restore your wisdom completely.

We do not need to know the specific methods for putting change into practice. So long as we sincerely wish to change and our resolve is firm, our subconscious will draw to us the ‘causes and conditions’ of change, letting us change as conditions come.

Each of our thoughts, each word and each deed, can resonate with the world outside and have an effect. And our own greatest power lies in the ‘present moment.’ Our present thoughts and actions can determine our future; so let no one fear change, but strive with courage and vigor to root out every bad habit.
Your mind is a tool
A human being is not merely mind; beyond the mind there lie many undeveloped powers of wisdom and strength.

You may believe that your mind directs all your activities. We have always assumed so, and we are used to letting our minds think so; but then the mind naturally takes itself to be immense, and whatever it wants, you cannot help but obey. In truth, you can master your own mind and retrain it. If the mind is sincerely trained, it can become a useful tool that obeys you.

Once your mind has become your tool, you may use it however you wish. The mind you now use is only a habitual mind, and habits can be changed. We must be willing to change the mind, and to understand that it can be retrained and made into a positive tool.
Put your thoughts and ideas aside for a while, and simply consider this idea in all sincerity: “My mind can become my tool, and I may use it however I wish.”

Once you have decided on a new thought, everything in your future will come to pass accordingly; if you firmly insist that you cannot change a bad habit, then that too will become your fact. So we may as well use this tool, the mind, wisely, and tell ourselves clearly: “I feel that I can change, and that change is growing easier and easier.” This is no idle fancy; it is truly so.

A woman who had long suffered from insomnia told me that for years she had let herself, once in bed, turn over and over on the pillow the things she had gone through during the day; if someone had provoked her, she would relive the scene twice or three times over, thinking back and forth, dwelling on the pain, without end. So it was common for her to lie awake at midnight, and not rare for her to go a whole night without closing her eyes. She thought she could not help it, because neither her thoughts nor her sleep obeyed her command.

Later she followed my advice and took charge of her mind. As soon as she got into bed she told herself: “What must be thought about can wait until tomorrow.” “My brain is resting now.” Each time a tide of thought surged up, she pushed it away at once.
This method worked for her, and her insomnia was cured. She told me excitedly: “So I really can control my own mind.”

This example tells us that within us there is a very great power that we never brought into play before; once its might is brought into play, we will know that change is not difficult at all, and that once the first step is taken, it truly does grow easier and easier.

People often misunderstand, thinking that their minds control them, that they are helpless before themselves, that even complaint is of no use. That is a great mistake. In fact, we can control our minds and use them as we use tools; it is enough that you do not compromise with bad habits. If you indulge yourself and keep thinking, “How difficult change is!” your power of control will be lost. You must say to yourself: “Everything about me lies in my own hands. There is nothing I cannot accomplish. If others can change, so can I.”

Everyone knows that drug addiction is a most serious matter, for drugs create addiction, and once addicted, a person is finished. The money he earns is never enough to buy drugs; he can no longer work, no longer keep his self-respect, and both mind and body are ravaged. Many people take one false step and regret it forever, unable to free themselves. Yet in this world there are also those who turn back from the sea of suffering and at last escape it. Such people are few, but they prove this much: for one who is willing to change, even drug addiction has no hold.

Human determination can conquer heaven” — this maxim has come down to us from ancient times. It tells us that all sovereignty lies in our own hands, and that even if we are fated to suffer, we can change our lives by doing good. As for petty bad habits, just give them up; why let them harm you for a whole lifetime? “Calamity and blessing have no gate; each person summons them for himself.” Do you wish to summon calamity or blessing? It is entirely up to you.

Still, change, though not impossible, is not so very easy either. For all our bad habits were formed not in this life alone; some are accumulated tendencies from former lives. So besides resolving to change, we must truly be prepared to put in more effort.

Determination comes first; perseverance to the end is essential. Which addict has never tried to quit? But they did not persevere to the end, and so they failed. Persevere to the end, and there is no way that quitting can fail.

Imagine that you have a small child, and you have always let him go to bed whenever he liked, but now you suddenly change your mind: he must go to bed at eight o’clock every night without fail. Under this new rule, what do you think the child will do at eight o’clock on the first night? He may rebel against the rule, and may even cry and make a scene. Is that not so? If your heart softens, if you cannot make up your mind, and you excuse him this once, then your child will use tears and tantrums to control you from then on, and will never obey your rules.

On the contrary, if you calmly explain to the child that this rule is for his own good and that he must obey it, then his rebellion will grow less and less. Two or three days after he goes to bed on time, he will be quite used to it, and from then on his daily routine will have changed.

Our minds are like that child. If you want to change them, at first they will certainly want to rebel and will not wish to be retrained. Remember, the one with the power of control is you. If you are focused and firm, and are not shaken by that mind, then before long you will have formed a new set of thoughts and behavior as you wished.
If you can recognize that you are not the victim of your thoughts but the master of your mind, then you will feel very happy, very happy indeed.
Practicing Relaxation
As you take in what I am saying, take a deep breath and practice relaxation at the same time.

First, breathe in deeply, and then breathe out. As you exhale, relax as much as you can and slow down, leaving not the slightest tension, as if you were completely at leisure. Let the top of your head, your forehead, and the muscles of your face all relax completely. (Even in ordinary times your head does not need to be tense, especially when you are reading. On the contrary, if your head is relaxed, you will find reading comfortable and easy.)

Next, relax your tongue, your throat, and your shoulders. Your arms and hands should relax too. Even if you are holding a book, there is no need to use deliberate force. Then relax your back, your stomach, and your abdomen
one place at a time. Let your deep breathing bring you a feeling of great ease and peace.
Finally, relax your legs and your feet. When you have done this, your whole body will be relaxed, very different from before.

You will now understand that your body had been tense all along. It was you who held your body so tense, which shows that you held your mind just as tense. When you are completely relaxed, you can tell yourself: “I am no longer tense now. I have let tension go, and let all fear go too; I need no longer resent, no longer feel uneasy, no longer grieve. All those feelings that made me unhappy I have let drift far away in relaxation. I am now very much at ease, and I feel good and safe about my life and my surroundings.”

Please repeat this practice two or three times every day. Enjoy again and again that light and joyful feeling after relaxation. If troubling thoughts arise, you may do this practice at any time to drive them away, so that you bathe always in ease and joy.
Each period of relaxation is best kept to about fifteen minutes.

When you do this practice, you may lean back in a chair and sit comfortably. When all your muscles, from top to bottom, are relaxed, you can imagine that you are on a beach: the sunlight is warm, a gentle breeze blows, and the waves come from far away to the front of your body, pass through you, and continue on. You need not avoid them; they come from afar and go far away. Those waves and your slow deep breathing keep a harmonious rhythm, so that all worldly thoughts vanish, as if you were within the shelter of the Buddha’s compassionate light.
Whoever does this relaxation practice will benefit the body: it can prevent illness before it comes and cure illness once it has come.
Appropriate Release

If a person can relax in ordinary times, and can find release when his mood is bad, that is a great help in life. Sometimes an appropriate outburst is of great benefit too. I had one such experience many years ago.

Once, both my shoulders suddenly began to ache, and the pain went on for two days. At first I thought it would pass on its own, and paid it no attention, but after several days the pain was still there. At last I had to sit up and ask myself: “Just what is wrong? Why does it hurt like this all the time?” The feeling was like fire, and the taste of it was hard to bear. I thought my pain must have been caused by resentment.

For a time I could not understand myself, and did not know where my resentment came from. So I took the two big pillows on the bed and gave them vent — I pounded those two big pillows with all my strength. When I had struck them a dozen times or so, I suddenly understood why I had resentment. I could only go on and on, pounding those pillows harder and harder.
When I had finished, I felt much better, and after that the pain in my shoulders actually did not return.

Many people do not know how to release their feelings and only hold them in, which does nothing for the ills that a bad mood stirs up. Many people are unhappy to this day over things that happened in the past. They are unhappy because in the past they did not do a certain thing, or did it wrong; or because they once possessed something and have now lost it; some were once hurt in love and will not accept love again; when they met with unpleasant things in the past, they concluded that those unpleasant things would come back again.
Some, because they were once deceived, are still afraid of dealing with people today, and are all the less able to forgive those who deceived them.
Others grieve to this day only because, when young, they were rejected and mocked by classmates.
There are those, unhappily divorced, who feel their life is forever incomplete.
And those who, having failed in love once, will never again enter the gate of romance.
Still others once stole something, and though they never repeated the offense, they go on punishing themselves ever after.

They do not know that clinging to what happened in the past only brings them more pain. The past is past; no one can change it now. If we cling to “the past” and refuse to let it go, then our thoughts have left “the present moment,” and can no longer concentrate or change our lives.

The Buddha said: “The sea of suffering is boundless; turn the head and the shore is there.” This “turning the head” means not clinging, but changing. On the contrary, if you do not change, you will only sink forever in the sea of suffering.

Yes, it is quite possible that we ourselves stumbled and fell into the sea, and quite possible that we were pushed in. Falling in was not our fault in the first place; but if we make no effort to return from the sea to the shore, and if someone clearly wants to save us and we will not listen, then the fault is ours.

Everyone has resentment in his life, but resentment must be dissolved one by one and made to vanish without a trace. Never let it pile up one item upon another and bury yourself in a “heap of resentment,” embittered for a whole lifetime.

We must clear away the dregs in our thinking, so that they no longer linger in our minds and make us unhappy. Think it through: it is really only garbage, and it can no longer exert any power to harm us. Why then hold on to it? That stick with which someone once beat us — we should kick it away, fling it far off, and forget it forever.

A ancient worthy said: “All memories are poisonous, whether the memory be painful or sweet.” A person can “remember” without having to “reminisce.” If we can let go of our reminiscences of the past, we live in “the present moment,” and can enjoy life and open up a beautiful future.

Take a sheet of paper and write down all the past events that entangle and trouble you. When you have finished, you may as well ask yourself: Have I the determination to let these old matters fade into forgetfulness? Just how am I to transcend them? Do I think I should be ruled by them forever? Can I not do more useful things to drive away these poisonous memories? Why can others let unhappy old matters fade, while I cannot?
When we ourselves have done wrong and failed, there is no need to blame ourselves. What can be made good, try to make good; what cannot be made good, let it go altogether, and never touch it again.

Before the Buddha you may state your intention, saying that you have recognized your error and will never commit it again. If you are truly sincere and truly transcend the mistake, all living beings will hear your repentance, forgive you, and help you grow again.
Forgiving Others Is Just as Important

If someone has hurt us, he will surely feel guilt and remorse; never think of revenge again. Remember: blows exchanged in grievance never end. Besides, revenge only deepens the pain of the wound, and is far inferior to pardoning others with a heart of great compassion.

A Chinese sage said: “Do not do to others what you would not have them do to you.” If we ourselves have wronged others, we naturally hope they will forgive us rather than take revenge. Since we do not wish to suffer revenge, we certainly may not take revenge on others. If you can act thus, your conduct is nothing less than that of a bodhisattva, and you will naturally win the praise of all beings; your body too, because of these good thoughts, will give off a kind of joyful light that often draws auspicious and fortunate conditions.
You are not only a good disciple of the Buddha; one day you yourself can become a Buddha.

Lay down the butcher’s knife and become a Buddha on the spot” — you know this saying. If you do not forgive others and want revenge, it is as though you held a butcher’s knife in your hand. Evil thoughts in the mind make your body give off an evil light, and that light is the readiest to attract evil forces, making you commit evil deeds. This you must surely avoid.

Greed, anger, and delusion” are what the Buddha called the three poisons. All manner of bad things develop from these three poisons; think it over carefully and you will confirm that the Buddha spoke nothing but the truth. Business failure and loss of money often come from greed; wrong choices, choosing the wrong partner, keeping bad company, and doing wrong things often come from delusion; destruction and crime often come from hatred. All human faults are inseparable from these three causes: greed, anger, and delusion.
Commit these three poisons once, and you suffer a loss once. Not forgiving others is precisely the poison of anger; and this poison, after it stabs another, usually turns back and stabs oneself.

Every one of us who walks the path of practice knows how important it is to forgive others. Before we are able to forgive others completely, we may as well do a certain contemplation; this contemplation can help us clear away the thought of revenge.

First, close your eyes, then think of the person hardest of all to forgive. What do you want to do with him? What would it take for you to forgive him? Do you want him to suffer before you can forgive him? If so, you can imagine him suffering, suffering in many ways; when you have finished imagining, you cannot help but feel compassion for him, and you will magnanimously pardon him, no longer wishing for revenge, no longer wishing to make him suffer so.
This contemplation should be done only once in a while, not every day. When you have finished it, you should from then on forgive this person and forever put away the thought of revenge.
Forgiveness

There are some people who find it very hard to forgive others completely. They may forgive for a little while, and afterward think again of the other’s faults and forgive no more. If that is so, you may try reciting the "Sutra for Dissolving Grievances" a few times.
The text of the “
Sutra for Dissolving Grievances” is very simple, yet its power is considerable. It seems able to call back the generosity and wisdom a person has lost.
The text runs:

Jinchi jinchi zhen jinchi, I now dissolve the jinchi for you, and never again bind the jinchi for you. Om! Strongest of the strong, most auspicious of the auspicious; in the assembly of Pāra there is surpassing benefit. May all hostile spirits depart from my body. Mahāprajñāpāramitā.”
Recite it over and over in this way until your mind has no hindrance and your breath is calm and your spirit at ease.

It is very efficacious and very useful. You may recite it while doing other things; you need not sit still to recite. It will help drive away those tormenting memories, driving them far off, so that they no longer disturb your mood.
You are the strongest of the strong, the most auspicious of the auspicious; never again will you be harmed by those shadows.
I believe that the more you recite it, the more powerful you will become, like Mount Tai that no one can overthrow.
When you recite, do so softly, so that you can hear yourself, and the faster you recite the better, as though you were swiftly sending out many beams of golden light, before which all shadows flee.

There are also some people who do not know how to forgive themselves. They can never forget: a certain thing was done wrong and brought very bad consequences; a certain thing wronged someone and caused that person pain
In such a case, the first thing is always to be able to speak in your own defense; since you are generous with others, you should be generous with yourself as well.

A fault is the result of an action, not its motive. No one in the world intends to harm himself or intends to harm others. There was a young man of seventeen who, while learning to drive, struck and killed a little boy who ran across the road in front of his car. Ever after, he brooded over it with great guilt. In fact, he had never intended to kill that little boy; he was only learning to drive when the boy suddenly ran across the road, giving him no time to swerve, and so the accident happened. This was not the fault of the young learner at all. Why should he lay the blame upon himself? He should speak in his own defense, telling others and telling himself that this truly was not his fault. Of course there is bound to be shock, but there is no need at all for inward guilt.
Seal Up Old Matters; Do Not Touch Them

Tell yourself that you can do it. In fact, everyone can do it; as long as you do not indulge yourself in forcing your way down a blind alley, you can leave those long-sealed old matters completely untouched.

In ordinary, quiet times we can imagine that we are a child of five or six. You see this child, and you gaze deeply into his eyes; he seems to be longing for something. As you go on gazing deeply, you will find that the one thing the child asks of you is that you love him. You imagine yourself reaching out your arms to embrace this child, holding him tenderly in arms full of love, telling him that you love him very much and appreciate him; telling him that it is all right if he makes mistakes while learning; telling him that whatever happens, you will be at his side.

Then imagine that this child is shrinking, shrinking until he is small enough for your heart to hold him, small enough to be placed within your heart. Each time you look into your own heart, you can see this child’s little face looking at you. You must go on cherishing him and giving him boundless love.

Then imagine your mother. She seems very frightened, because she needs love and does not know where to find it. At once you reach out your arms and embrace your mother, telling her that you love her and care for her deeply; telling her that she can lean on you, that you will go on loving her and caring for her. When you see your mother beginning to grow calm and no longer afraid, you shrink her too, until she is small enough to be held in your heart. Put your mother also into your heart, together with your own small self. Let the two little ones cherish each other.

Then think of your father. He seems very sad and very frightened, and very much wishes someone to love him. Imagine him sighing without end, utterly at a loss. You now know how to cherish a frightened person, so quite naturally and easily you reach out your arms and hold your father, letting him feel your love, letting him know that if he has any problem or difficulty, you will be at his side caring for him.

When your father is no longer sorrowful and has begun to be happy, you shrink him too, until he is small enough to be held in your heart. Put the little him into your heart as well, and with the little mother and the little self, let the three be together, let them cherish one another, while you at the same time give boundless love to all three.

If you already have a spouse and children, then in the same way let the little versions of them be placed in your heart along with everyone else. You are the tree, your parents are your roots, your spouse and children are your branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit. All of you need the fertile soil of love, the sunlight of love, the rain and dew of love
The power of love is very great; it shines within your heart, filling you with peace and with joy. The power of love can transform your thoughts and clear away your bad habits.
I do not want to be fat
I do not want to be poor
I do not want to grow old
I do not want to live here
I do not want this romance
I do not want to be like my parents
I do not want to be stuck in this job
I do not want my present hair, nose, and body
I do not want to be lonely
I do not want to be sad
I do not want to be sick

The sentences above are the ones we habitually use. We think that so long as we fight against the negative we will get a positive result, but this is entirely wrong. We are always blaming ourselves, yet blaming cannot change us, nor bring us happiness and positivity. On the contrary, if we spend too much time fighting the negative, we will spiral into the whirlpool of negativity and never reach the positive shore; more than that, we will create still more negativity and be wholly trapped inside it.
We should put our attention on the positive side. Then the sentences above will become:
I am not too fat.
I have enough money.
I always feel young.
I am moving to another place to live right now.
I have a very happy love relationship.
I am myself, not my parents.
I like my hair, my nose, and my body.
I am full of love. I am happy and free.
My body is very healthy.

We must learn to make our wishes on the positive side. We are used to speaking negatively, for example: “I hate my job.” This sentence, though it states a fact, will not help us progress, because it is negative. The truly positive way to say it should be: “I think I will soon find a very good new job.” If you speak in this way, your mood will open up, and it is truly possible that you will find a new job that suits you very well.

We should keep making positive wishes, and must no longer be as before, used to speaking negative words. If for a time we still cannot turn ourselves around, then let us begin from “the present moment.” In short, we no longer let the negative side manipulate us.

When we make a wish, we should not say “I hope” or “I want,” but “I can.” For “hope” and “want” are neither as powerful nor as confident as “I can.” “Hope” is often very faint, and what one wants is often not obtained; only what one “can” do is certainly done.

We should especially appreciate ourselves; we may even often tell ourselves in our hearts: “I appreciate myself,” and the more often the better. Whenever you notice that you are about to slide toward negative thinking, remind yourself all the more, telling yourself: “I appreciate myself.” In this way you can bring your own hidden potential into play on the positive side. None of us knows how much potential we have hidden; how can we just casually give up on ourselves?

Winston Churchill, the British prime minister famous throughout the world, was a very dull child when young. He once said of himself: “On the whole, school life was rather depressing for me. Everyone of about my age seemed far stronger than I in games and in lessons. To be left behind at the very start of every race — that was truly hard to bear.”

When he turned twelve, poor examination results placed him in the lowest form of the basic class at Harrow, and for nearly a year afterward he remained in that inglorious position. Clever students took both Greek and Latin; he could not.

His class was regarded by the school as a “cow-herding class,” fit only to study the native language, English. And he was the dullest student in that class; even for English alone he needed three times as long as the others, and he had still not finished the third form. Moreover, he never managed to leave Harrow with a lower-school diploma.

Think about it: if Churchill had then been downcast and blamed himself, if he had not appreciated himself, how could his later achievements ever have come about? Each of us has potential just as Churchill did, and so long as it is used well, anyone can become a great person. So you must tell yourself this, and believe in yourself.

Every one of us is different; each has his own unique character, and this is where each person is precious. Nature never repeats herself: every drop of rain differs from every other drop; every snowflake differs from every other snowflake; every flower differs from every other flower; and the fingerprints of each of us differ from everyone else’s. We need not do things the way others do them, nor may we measure all people by a single standard.

We need not even compete with others or compare ourselves to them, and still less need we become like them; that would only injure our own particular spirit. We came into this world precisely to express our own unique character.

Before I learned to appreciate myself, I did not know what I could really do; only after I learned to appreciate and love myself did I feel how meaningful my own unique character is, and how fully it can be brought into play.

Like the psychologist William James, I believe: “Your faith will help to create the fact.” This is very close to what Buddhism says: destiny lies in our own hands, and even one fated to birth and death and rebirth can, through practice, awaken at once and attain the liberation of nirvāṇa.

People do sometimes feel a sense of failure, but when you fall you can stand up and walk on. Failure is in fact not a hundred percent bad thing: the reason people fail is mostly that they attempted something beyond their capacity — and that is exactly what a person ought to attempt.
As the saying goes, failure is the mother of success. Draw experience and lessons from failure, and you will not fail again; not only will you not fail again, you will bring about success.

There is a South African proverb: “Every calamity is the root of blessing.” Buddhism says: “Affliction is itself bodhi (wisdom).” A person who has never passed through hardship will certainly not be a person of achievement. When a problem comes, face it and deal with it; if the old methods do not work, find new ones. If you cannot think of new methods yourself, go and ask a friend, ask your parents, ask an expert — three cobblers’ wits combined equal one Zhuge Liang. If all else fails, try the wondrous power of “sitting meditation”; it can bring forth “wisdom” from “concentration” and let you think of a way to solve the problem.

If a person had no spirit of out with the old and in with the new, how could he know the joy of turning defeat into victory? The pain of being reborn is worth gritting your teeth and enduring; besides, that pain is by no means lasting, and when you stand firm, help from all sides will begin to reach out to you.

A single small tomato seed is not to be despised.
