You need only plant it in the soil, give it the right air, sunlight, water, and fertilizer, and it can grow from a tiny sprout breaking through the earth into branches and leaves; and if you also know how to prune the branches and pinch off the tips, then in the space of a few short months it will bear you dozens or even a hundred tomatoes, letting you see your achievement and reap a harvest. What is more, your happiness begins on the very day it sprouts, and all the work thereafter is done in happiness. Only at the moment of transplanting it into the soil are you hesitant and anxious, fearing that after the transplant the tomato plant will die. And if on the soil where you mean to plant tomatoes something else is already growing, and you must first pull it out, you may be all the more afraid to begin.

Everything is hard at the beginning. But without a beginning, how can there be a harvest? So please drive out all your negative beliefs, the way you would pull up weeds from the soil and clear away the stones in the earth. And please do not say again:
My life is a mess.’
I ought to have plastic surgery.’
No one loves me.’
I have no good place to live.’
I hate my work.’
I do not know how to make use of my life.’
I am busy all day long, yet I never get enough done.’
I am not as good as other people.’
You can turn all those negative thoughts into positive ones. You can think like this:
I will dissolve the negative thoughts that make me unhappy.’
I have a sound body, and my face is not ugly.’
I meet love everywhere I go.’
Having a place to live is already good enough.’
I have the chance to find more satisfying work.’
I will put my life to good use.’
I appreciate everything I do.’
I love and admire myself.’

One shriveled tomato seed can become dozens and hundreds of tomatoes, red and large and delicious; how much more so we who are fully human? “He who escapes great calamity will surely know later blessing”: if even great calamity need not be feared, why fear a passing difficulty? “Heaven helps those who help themselves.” If you are willing to strive with all your heart, a miracle may well appear tomorrow — and you can hold this confidence today.

If you bend to your work today, tonight you will reap a harvest; when bad luck ends, good luck is sure to begin. The old and the past have already influenced our lives, but we can make them cease to act; we can make good use of ‘this present moment’ and create a brand-new life.

Think the Buddhadharma through carefully, and put it into practice. The Buddha’s teaching is the most perfect philosophy of life, and we can rely on it in both spirit and action. At the same time, we should keep company with friends who benefit us, and all the more should we eat the foods that benefit us and drink the drinks that benefit us — best of all, eat vegetarian and never touch alcohol.

A form of exercise suited to us is likewise something we need; exercise makes our muscles and bones strong and our blood flow smooth, and it also strengthens the heart and boosts resistance to illness. Swimming, t’ai chi, yoga, walking, and so on — any of these may be chosen.

Sitting in meditation can settle our minds and nurture our inner wisdom, so everyone should practice it. I practice sitting meditation every day too. When I close my eyes, I say to myself: ‘What is it that I need to know right now?’ Having asked, I sit quietly and wait for the answer. If the answer comes at once, so much the better; if it does not, that is no problem either — it will naturally come in a few days.

We can also practice more profound meditation techniques, and we can recite the Buddha’s name; we can even go and visit temples — all of which benefit body and mind. We must actively attain balance in the three areas of spirit, mind, and body; we cannot neglect any one of them, for if we neglect any one, we cannot be balanced, and we cannot truly benefit.
I enjoy learning new skills.’
If a small child fell down while learning to walk and then refused to try again, he would never learn to walk, and would never know how very easy walking actually is.

Each of us is like a small child learning to walk: whatever we begin to learn also requires a great deal of practice before it succeeds. First of all we need great attention and concentration, and through the whole process we must not think of it as difficult; we must see what we are learning as something new and interesting, and learn it carefully. The process of learning is always the same: whether you learn to drive, to type, to play ball, or to cultivate new positive thoughts, you will meet with many difficulties at the start. But if we keep at it and overcome those difficulties, it will come to feel easy, with no difficulty left at all. You might remind yourself again and again: ‘I am doing my very best.’
When we begin to learn anything new, of course we feel very timid, because we have no experience and do not know whether we can do it well.
Support yourself and carry on with great confidence; even if our beginning is not brilliant, later on we will surely succeed.

I remember my first lecture. When I had finished speaking and stepped down from the platform, I thought of nothing else; secretly I only supported and comforted myself, saying: ‘That went quite well! It was the first time, after all; if I speak a few more times, I will surely do better.’

After I sat down, I thought of several points that needed improving in future lectures. I absolutely did not criticize myself for that first talk; I only supported my own performance. I am afraid that if I had stepped down and torn my lecture to pieces — scolding myself for being useless, for making this mistake and that mistake
then I might never have dared to give a second lecture, and even if I had to walk up onto the platform again, I would surely have felt especially timid and nervous.

I supported myself without growing smug; so I could improve, and of course my later results were better. And so it proved: at my second lecture I was already much more practiced and much improved, and not the least bit stage-frightened.

I once bought a computer and set about learning to use it. Such a thing as a computer is truly marvelous. Learning to use it was not without difficulty at first, but as I kept at it, once I had learned, it proved so useful that it was almost like magic — thoroughly delightful. Yet if I had not learned it properly and used it wrongly, then it would have been good for nothing at all, and quite another story.

In the course of learning, I sometimes felt dejected and lost patience; but seeing the computer sitting quietly on the desk, waiting for me to discover its uses, I was at once filled with fresh energy, took a new interest in it, and in the end mastered it completely and learned it well, so that it became a great helper to me.

I think that everyone who studies the Buddha’s teaching shares much the same experience: at the very beginning, everyone finds it hard — not easy to carry out all that the Buddha taught, and not merely difficult but even impossible. Yet as one keeps studying, the impossible becomes possible, and the difficult becomes easy.
My Daily Routine

My daily routine goes like this: when I wake in the morning, before my eyes are even open, I thank the Buddha in my heart, and all the people I can think of, and everything. Then I go to bathe. After my bath I spend half an hour sitting in meditation and reciting sutras. Then I do about fifteen minutes of exercise, and eat breakfast: breakfast consists of fruit or fruit juice, and an herbal tea without caffeine.
I am truly grateful to have enough food. I am grateful to the farmers and merchants who grow and make the food, and to the people who have helped my life in some way.

Before lunch I go and look in the mirror to see whether my face is glowing. If I am free of illness and pain and full of vigor, I am content, and feel that the day is truly a happy one; that I can know everything and do what I want to do and build up some achievement — all of it is so perfect.

My lunch is usually the plainest food, needing little thought to cook. When I come home from work in the afternoon, I relax all the muscles of my body and quietly listen to some tapes that suit my mood.

Supper too is only some grains and vegetables, though now and then I eat something else. I know that my body is suited only to simple food. I very much enjoy having supper with others, and chatting with them afterward, exchanging what we have learned.

On Sundays or rest days, when I have time to read and review, I am always full of interest. There is so much for a person to learn — endless, inexhaustible. When I receive a special inspiration, I write it down in a notebook, as though putting a precious object into a safe, making sure it will not be lost.

Before I sleep, I sit in meditation for fifteen minutes, recite the Buddha’s name for half an hour, and review the day’s experiences; then I tell myself: to stretch out every limb and lie down to rest is a comfort beyond compare. I no longer carry my thoughts to bed with me, because my brain, like my limbs, needs rest too.
I often sleep soundly until dawn, rise at daybreak, and joyfully welcome the new day.

My daily routine is thus well ordered, and seems to be more than most people could manage. Yet I do it every day, adapting myself to my new thoughts, and it is as simple and easy to handle as brushing my teeth and washing my face, and can be done very naturally. I think that if I had a family and needed to live with them, I could carry out the same routine as above, and it would even be livelier, more interesting, and more beneficial.

I feel that the two periods of sitting meditation, morning and evening, are indispensable for everyone, because sitting meditation can make us feel at peace, bring body and mind into balance, and fill a person with positive drive. Even if one is truly too busy to find time for sitting, one should still manage to make time for it, at least once a day. Sitting meditation gives our mind comfort and training, and can also increase our wisdom, bringing us closer to the Buddha.

When a person first learns to sit in meditation, he need only sit for five minutes. Sit quietly and observe your breathing, and let all your thoughts go. If thoughts arise, pay them no attention; they will disappear of themselves.

Our mind is accustomed to thinking, so when we first sit in meditation thoughts will appear: there is no need to destroy them; simply let them pass by naturally, and that is enough. Nowadays there are many places all over the world where one can learn sitting meditation, and books on it are available for purchase. Whatever difficulties arise at the beginning, they are no problem; once you are used to it, you will grope your way to the most ideal method of sitting.

I usually sit quietly and first ask myself: ‘What do I need to know?’ Then I stop thinking. The answer often appears by itself after the sitting is over. Or perhaps it may come a little later — one never knows. I believe that my own subconscious is already brewing the right answer. Sitting in meditation is the best way for oneself to communicate with one’s subconscious, and for oneself to communicate with the Buddha.

The common method of sitting meditation is to sit quietly and silently count your own breaths. As you breathe in, count one; as you breathe out, count two; go on counting up to ten, then return to one and begin again from one. If you find that many thoughts have arisen and thrown all your counting into confusion, then count from one again and fend off the random thoughts.
There are also times when you find that after counting to ten you are still unconsciously counting eleven, twelve
then you can simply stop at once and begin counting again from one.
Your Daily Routine
Let me ask you once more: when you get up in the morning, what is the first thing you want to say to yourself?

Each day we have different things we want to say. Are the things you want to say positive or negative? What I want to say now is all positive; but long ago, when I got up in the morning I said negative things too: ‘Ah, another day!’ I would sigh in my heart.

In those days I often greeted the new day with such negative words, so my whole self was negative every day as well. But now, when I get up, I thank the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and all the more I thank everything beautiful in the world. After rising I resolve that this day will surely be a day full of meaning and full of happiness; every one of my days is lived positively and joyfully.
Try to think: what is your own daily routine like?

Long ago there was a woman who never married her whole life. In her time women did not go out to work, so she could only depend on her father and brothers and live at others’ mercy. Her days were of course far from easy, yet she managed to live remarkably well. When she was young her sweetheart suddenly fell ill and died, and even such terrible news could not strike her down; she lived happily to the age of eighty-five and passed away in peace.

In the notebook she left behind, her niece discovered the rules of living she had set for herself: she required herself to do five things every day, and only thus was she able to be happy and serene her whole life. Those five things she had to do were:
1. Do something beneficial to others.
2. Do something beneficial to yourself.
3. Do something you do not want to do but ought to do.
4. Exercise the body.
5. Exercise the mind.

Her diary recorded in detail how she carried out those five necessary things: she cared for others every day, and did embroidery and sewing for herself; she kept the whole household in good order; she walked to the neighboring village; and she read helpful books every day. It turns out that in this way she waged war against the darkness. In her diary she wrote:
I myself take the initiative and escape the “prison of the self.”’

Where I am rooted, there I grow strong and flourish.’ This lady might well have ended her days in gloom, yet she handled her life exceedingly well, and so was not swallowed up by the darkness. Her times were ancient, but her method, her perseverance, and her positivity remain an excellent example for us modern people.
None of us lives exactly as we would wish, but if we can strive positively and make every day meaningful and happy, then we gain a happy life, a happy lifetime, and even a happy life to come.

I know why I used to be filled with negative thoughts early every morning, and I know that all unhappy people are the same, for this reason: there is a difficult problem in the heart. As long as that problem is not solved, the person is unhappy.

From the perspective of my present professional knowledge, putting off the solution of a difficult problem is the most wasteful thing one can do with a life; it makes a person unable to concentrate on his work while working, and dazed in mind during his leisure.

The way to deal with it is this: begin at once to solve your difficult problem. If you can solve it all at once, so much the better; if not, then begin to solve it step by step. Solve as much as you can, and once you are solving it step by step, the burden on your heart will lighten step by step; once a person is on the road, he need no longer worry about the future.

Many people are also unhappy because the day’s affairs are too many. They wake at dawn, and before their eyes are even open they discover that inside and out, great and small, countless matters are waiting for them to do; so they feel unbearably vexed and utterly dispirited, and are filled with negative, unhappy thoughts.

In fact, they could arrange things the night before: write down on a sheet of paper the things that must be done, strike out the things that can be left undone, and free up time for recreation and rest. Then they would not feel oppressed; instead they would have a sense of achievement at having arranged things well, and their hearts would naturally be happy; and when they opened their eyes in the morning they would not be fretful.

As for being troubled over money matters and having one’s mood affected by it, one need only increase income and reduce expenditure, earn more, spend less, and not buy things at random. The problem is really not hard to solve.

Broken-hearted in love? Think it through, and in fact there is no need to grieve at all. When two people part because they are not suited to each other, that is a perfectly reasonable outcome; must those who do not get along force themselves to stay together? Is that not the most twisted and absurd way of doing things? No one would wish to have a great boil on his body and refuse to have it treated; unsuitable partners and painful love are more dreadful than a great boil — why not be rid of them quickly?

Within ten paces there is sure to be fragrant grass’: the right person is right beside you, waiting for you to discover him. Welcome each day gladly; your true love is there amid the crowd, and you may rise and go looking — they are waiting for you to begin!’

Those who suffer bodily illness cannot sleep well at night, and after daybreak there is pain here and discomfort there, so of course they feel negative and full of bad feelings about the new day. In fact, illness is only a temporary physiological phenomenon, not something permanent, so there is no need to be pessimistic; to accept what comes with equanimity and keep an optimistic mind not only makes the illness easier to cure, but also makes life much easier for one’s family.

Only as a child, when I had a headache and a fever, did I feel as though doomsday were at hand. After I grew up, I learned that a fever means the body is doing battle with illness, and that pain is a message meant to draw your attention; so I could take it calmly, and sometimes I even counted ‘a small illness as a blessing’ — lying in bed resting with nothing at all to do is, after all, a rare opportunity, and no reason at all to be negative. Moreover, when an illness stops worsening, it is already easing; to savor that eased feeling thoroughly — how could it not fill one with gratitude?

Remember the Buddha’s instruction: every fruit must have its cause. There is nothing to complain of. If you decide that the present fruit is too bitter, you can at once find a way to plant wholesome causes, and then you can turn the bitter fruit around.
Every morning when you open your eyes, plan what good deeds you can do that day, and then carry them out one by one; this can improve your mood.

Are you suffering? Think of those who suffer more than you. Many of them live amid war and chaos, where at any moment they may be killed, living in terror, without a moment’s peace. Some are in places struck by natural disaster or man-made calamity, on the brink of starvation, unable even to get a meal of the coarsest food to fill their bellies. Some, from poverty and sickness, are skin and bones, barely breathing

Can you still not be satisfied? Do you still want happiness to fall from the sky? Well fed and well dressed, refusing to strive, and meanly pitying yourself — will that bring you the help of a benefactor?
Be content with what you have, and do not chase after what you lack; then you will be grateful, and every morning you can be happy.

The woman of the old days mentioned above lived in unhappy circumstances, but because she set herself five things to do each day and carried them out thoroughly, she overcame her suffering and lived her whole life in happiness. We may well take her as our example and set rules for ourselves each day, carrying them out strictly; then we too will surely reap as she did.
Turning Suffering into Joy
Imagine that you have already become the self you idealize; as far as you can, feel, see, touch, and hear with this new self. Observe how people respond to you — do they very much like this new you?

Whatever others’ response to you may be, do not waver; continue your new life. You can read more Buddhist books to understand yourself, understand others, and understand this dusty world, and you can also consult all kinds of other books to broaden your knowledge. There are many very useful books in the world — as the saying goes, ‘opening a book is always profitable.’ To rebuild your life, the first step is to cultivate yourself in the spiritual dimension.
Listen more to others’ opinions, take more useful courses, and discuss or study together more often with people of like interests.

Walking the spiritual path is a lifelong necessity. The more you learn, the more you know; learning has no end. If you can practice in daily life what you have learned, then as the days go by your life will change, full of vigor and meaning.

You will also find that you can never become ugly and never grow old; many people who have cultivated themselves to a high degree in spirit, though old, look white-haired with a child’s face, and show no sign of decline at all. You must love yourself, love your character, and love what you do.
In daily life, laugh as much as you can. Then the shadow of negativity will no longer have any hold on you.
Perhaps in your next life you will completely change your attitude toward being human — but why not begin that work of change in this very life?

There was a man named Luo Min Ka Chen who was diagnosed with a terminal illness; he often joked about himself with great humor, and went on laughing and talking with others as usual, and so his terminal illness was cured. Later he contracted another terminal illness, and he still went on with his humorous ways, laughing together with others; in the end this second terminal illness was also cured without medicine!
A person’s illness has a great deal to do with his state of mind; one who stays optimistic can keep a hundred illnesses at bay, and even a terminal illness will again and again vanish and depart.

Everyone, when going to sleep at night, can close his eyes and give thanks for all that he has gained this day, and give thanks for the Buddhas’ and Bodhisattvas’ protection. Doing so can make life fuller still, with a lucky star always shining overhead.

I feel that before going to sleep at night one should not watch the news on television or listen to the news on the radio, because such news reports tell of one disaster after another; carrying all these negative things into one’s dreams is truly of no benefit.

Good dreams can help dissolve many of life’s disappointments, and can also help you resolve the questions you need answered, leaving a person full of energy on waking; bad dreams have the opposite power, and leave one dejected. So to avoid carrying unhappy things to bed is the wiser course.
When sleeping, a person should have a peaceful mind, hold positive convictions, and trust the way life unfolds. Sleeping in this way will not only bring proper rest, but also bring ease and joy.

There is one more point we should truly put into practice: we must not regard work as a bitter thing. In fact all work is very enjoyable and very interesting. A Western philosopher has a famous saying: ‘Think carefully, and you will find that amusement is really far more boring than work.’ It all depends entirely on your attitude.

A boy had just come home from school when his mother sent him to the field to pick half a basket of strawberries as fruit for the family after dinner; he went, unwilling and resentful. Walking along the road, he suddenly thought: why not pick a whole big basket, so that everyone could eat their fill and he could give his mother a surprise? No sooner had he thought this than he was filled with energy, his earlier displeasure swept away, and he was so excited that it was more pleasant than any game. He now intended to do twice the work his mother had asked of him, but because his outlook had changed, bitterness had turned to joy.
The more a person understands joy, the more he can dissolve his difficulties.

If you always treat your problems as though they were a comedy, then you will find them very amusing and very funny. In fact comedy and tragedy are the same thing; it depends entirely on your outlook. Every one of us has played the fool and done foolish things, and it is no great matter.
Do all you can to see the changes of life as pleasant and enjoyable. Here I bless you, and wish you ever more delight!
No human life is ever isolated; we stand in relation to everything, and the most important thing in life is precisely this relation of interdependence.
You are now in relation to this book, and you are in relation to my views as well. Your relations with other people, with your work, with objects, food, weather, means of transport

and so on, are at the same time a reflection of your relation with yourself. Your relation with yourself is largely shaped by your relations with adults in childhood; the way adults responded to you then becomes the way you respond to yourself today. Some of these responses are positive, and some are negative.

Think about it: when you blame yourself, are you using the same words your parents used when they blamed you? How did they praise you then? I can be sure that you are now praising yourself in those very same words.
If your parents never once praised you in childhood, then you do not know how to praise yourself, and may well think yourself good for nothing and wholly undeserving of praise.

I am not teaching you to blame your parents, because your parents’ parents were like that toward them in their day; they too were once victims, and so they did not know how to teach what they themselves had never known.

Experts say that our relationships with others all reflect our relationships with our father or mother. They also say that if we do not clarify these relationships, we will forever repeat the same pattern and never have truly ideal relationships with others.

In our human relationships we constantly reflect ourselves and those beliefs of ours. Whatever our employers, friends, lovers, or children may be like, we treat them all according to the beliefs we accumulated in our early years.

You will often dislike certain things about certain people; in fact those very things are what you yourself are doing, or what you wish to do. Truly, these people all match some trait in you — otherwise you would never keep them in your life at all.

You might observe that person in your life who dissatisfies you, and think of three things about him that you dislike, which you believe he needs to change. Then search deeply within yourself and see whether you too have the same three faults as he does. Ask yourself whether you have ever done the same improper things he has done.

Close your eyes and think this through carefully. If you actually discover that you behave just like the person you dislike, then ask yourself whether you are willing to change those bad things in yourself. If you can remove those bad habits and bad beliefs from your thinking, then you may ask others to change as well, or ask that they no longer appear in your life.

If your boss very much likes to criticize you and is deeply dissatisfied with you, then you should also search within yourself. Very likely on some psychological level you, like your boss, find it hard to accept others; or you have decided that all bosses like to criticize and are never satisfied with their subordinates’ performance, and your boss happens to be that sort of person. In fact, perhaps it is not so at all.

Conversely, if you are the boss and one of your employees often does not follow your instructions, then all the more should you search within yourself and see whether you have made some mistake. If you have, change those mistakes at once; that is more useful than firing the employee. Once you have clarified your own system of thought, you will find it easy to accept others.
If you have a colleague who often will not cooperate with you, you should search within yourself too, and think how many times you have refused to cooperate with him.
If you have a friend who is very unreliable and often disappoints you, you should likewise search within yourself and ask: have I ever been a disappointment to others?

If your sweetheart is cold as ice toward you and lacking in warmth, you might consider whether, in your childhood, your parents ever said, ‘Once love is satisfied, it cools’? It is this sentence that has influenced you, making you feel that your beloved is cold — when in fact she is not.

If your spouse often complains about you and gives you no support in many things, you should also think: were your father and mother likewise often complaining about each other and not supporting each other? Very likely, for this very reason, you complain about your spouse in just the same way.

If you have a child whose habits make you angry, I can guarantee that you yourself have exactly the same habits as that child. A child’s habits are formed by imitating the adults around him. As long as you clear away these bad habits in yourself, your child will quite naturally change as well.
There is only one way to change others, and that is to change ourselves first. Once we have changed our own system of thought, you will find that “they” have changed too.

Complaining is completely useless. Complaining about others only makes us lose our own strength, and we must at all costs hold on to our strength. If we have no strength, we have no power to change. Without the power to change, we will never find a way out.
About Love

When we do not deliberately seek love, nor even expect it, love very often appears quite naturally. Conversely, if we set our minds on finding a lover, then what we find will usually not be a suitable lover, and in the end we will only end up with the wrong person.

Love is not something floating outside us; it lies deeply hidden within our own hearts. So it cannot be sought here and there; rather, a special power must trigger it, and there is no need to want love at once. Perhaps you simply are not yet able to receive love; perhaps you have not yet developed to the point where you can attract the lover of your ideals.

You should not casually pick just anyone in order to fulfill your wish to have a lover. You should first have an ideal: what kind of lover do you really want? What kind of love do you wish for? You can write down on paper your wishes about love, and write down what qualities it should have. Then earnestly develop those qualities in yourself, and only so can you attract a lover who matches your expectations.

You may also ponder deeply: what is it, really, that has left you without a lover? Is your ideal too high? Are you too picky? Do you lack self-confidence? Do you want a love that is utterly out of the ordinary? Are you afraid of growing close to a lover? Have you decided that it is impossible for anyone to love you?

Love often comes suddenly. When it comes, you must be prepared: prepare a garden plot for love, prepare to water it. You must love others first, and then others will naturally love you; you must be able to open your heart, and to receive love.
I am content with all that I do.”
Is this wise saying also your ideal? Have the following thoughts set a limit on your contentment? Let us drag out into the light these thoughts that leave you dissatisfied —
You do not like your job
You hate your boss
You feel the pay you get is not enough
You feel your boss does not appreciate the results of your work
You do not get along with your colleagues
You do not know what it is you really like to do
All these thoughts are negative and wrong. If you think this way, how could you ever have a better position? An attitude like this cannot help you at all; it only makes your work miserable.

If you are truly deeply dissatisfied with your job, if you truly wish to change positions, if problems truly keep arising in your work, or if for the moment you simply cannot find another job, then the best thing to do is this:

First, keep the position you have now. Recognize that it is only a small stage on the road of your life. You do this work because you have a need for it. If the people in your office treat you badly and make you unhappy, you might ask yourself: is it because my own consciousness, my own thoughts, are causing others to be displeased with me?

Once you have found the cause, you should watch over your own mind and regard your present work with care — and even the job you held before — blessing them all with love. Toward your working environment — every place in it, every piece of equipment, every tool, every member of staff, every supervisor, every customer and the rest — you should sincerely offer blessing and love.

You should affirm to yourself: “I always work for very good supervisors.” “My supervisor always respects me and appreciates me.” “My supervisor is very open-hearted; working for him is easy.” You must keep these thoughts in your heart at all times, and when one day you yourself become a supervisor, then, in keeping with these beliefs, you will be a good supervisor to those under you.

I remember a young man who came to see me. He was about to begin a new job, yet he felt extremely nervous and full of anxiety. I said to him: “Why do you keep worrying that you will do poorly? In fact you can do very well, and be very successful. As long as you open your heart, let your talents come into play, bless your working environment, and fill your heart with love for your supervisors, your colleagues, and your customers, then everything will surely go smoothly.”
He did as I said, and afterward he was indeed very successful.

When we change jobs and resign from the one we had, we should also let go of that job with love, and bless the person who comes to take our place, hoping that he will enjoy the work and that he will succeed. In our society there are a great many jobs, needing people of every kind of talent. That we can work alongside others at a place of work, with one taking my place or me taking his, is a special karmic connection, and so it must be treasured.
Ordinarily, you should often think in this way:

I open my heart to accept this very good job; it is meaningful both for me and for society. In this work I can express myself through my gifts and my potential, and open up a sky of my own that satisfies me. I respect and love my colleagues, and they too all love and respect me. The working environment is ideal, and the wages I earn are quite reasonable.”

If someone among your colleagues makes you unhappy, you can bless that colleague with love. You should know that every one of us has two sides to his character: we can all do good, and we can all do evil; we can become a Buddha or a bodhisattva, and we can become a Hitler. That colleague who displeases you, though he criticizes you often, you can still be certain that within his heart there is also abundant love. Everyone has the Buddha-nature, so he too must have the Buddha-nature. If he is gloomy and unhappy now, you can be certain that this is only a passing phenomenon; afterward he can still be lively and happy. If he is full of ill will, you can believe that this is only a surface appearance, and that in his heart he is gentle and compassionate. If you do not look at others’ shortcomings but only at their strengths, then the person you have thus acknowledged will always show you his strengths.
So getting along with people is not difficult; you need only be able to praise their good points.

A man had found a new job playing the piano in an elegant restaurant. The owner of this restaurant was long known for being harsh and unkind, and everyone who worked there called him behind his back “the man with a heart of stone.” So this piano player came to ask my advice about what he should do.

I said to him: “Everyone has a good side within. How the other staff react to this boss is none of your concern. When you think of him, bless him with love; keep reminding yourself and affirming that your boss is a very good person. You need only repeat this affirmation, and that will be enough.”

After he heard my advice, he did as I had said. Before long his boss began to treat him very, very well, even giving him a share of the profits and helping him find part-time playing engagements elsewhere. But the staff who had always hated the boss were still treated harshly by him and still received the same old treatment, with no improvement at all.

An employee needs love toward his employer, and the same attitude should be brought to the amount of wages he receives. If you like your work but feel your pay is not enough, then you might, with a loving heart, bless both parties, and in time your pay will naturally increase. And if you are already content with your present pay, it too will naturally increase, making you more content still.

We should affirm that we can rise step by step and can earn higher wages; we should not be negative because we are now paid little. We should affirm that we truly have value and make a great contribution to the work, and so our employer will surely share with us the money he earns.
At work we should always do our utmost; then the boss will see the results and appreciate them, and will raise us from our present low position to a higher and better, ever higher and better one.

Not a few people in society have risen gradually from apprentice to manager. Effort is never wasted; success or failure, high or low, rests entirely with oneself. Because we ourselves are as we are now, we have the circumstances we have now. If we stand still, our circumstances stand still; if we improve, our circumstances improve. Cause and effect depend entirely on what we ourselves do, and there is not the slightest need to blame heaven or resent others.
Every experience is an achievement.”

What, after all, is called “failure”? Does it mean that what you did fell short of your ideal or your hope? The law of experience is always fair: if we express our thoughts and beliefs perfectly, we will not fail. When a person feels he has failed, it must be that he forgot to take each step that had to be taken; or that he lacked confidence in himself, thought he could never succeed again, and so abandoned the road he had not yet finished walking.

This is very much like my use of a computer. If I make some mistake in the course of using it, the result comes out wrong; the fault is not the computer’s but my own — it was I who did not give instructions according to the computer’s rules, and so the computer went wrong. To keep the computer from erring again, I must from now on learn more carefully and use it correctly.
With a thing that has not succeeded, you must keep on trying; do not stop until it succeeds.”

This saying is quite right. But it does not mean that you should keep bulling ahead, repeating the same mistaken methods as before; it means you should recognize your own mistakes and carry on by another method.
Keep shifting to a more correct method, until you can do it completely right.

I feel that when we come into this world, all of us have it in us to leap from success to greater success. If we cannot, it only means that what we do has not come into accord with our own ability; or that our self-confidence is too high and our effort too little; or, what is more, that we have already succeeded and do not know it.
Still, if we set our standards too high — so high that we are not yet capable of reaching them — then it is also possible that we will never succeed at all.

When a small child is learning to walk or to talk, we praise and encourage his every tiny bit of progress. The child’s eyes then shine with hope, and he does better each time. Do we likewise encourage ourselves when we are learning something new? Or do we, in the midst of our own learning, scold ourselves for being stupid, or call ourselves failures?

Many actors want their very first rehearsal to be flawless, with not one mistake. I tell them that the purpose of a rehearsal is to learn, and that in rehearsal it is quite all right to make mistakes — a rehearsal exists precisely so that the actors may learn and search out new and correct ways.

All of us must keep on learning if we are to gain new achievements; then these new achievements naturally become a part of us and accumulate. The expertise that many experts display is just the fruit they have gathered after long years of learning.

I too once refused to try anything new, because I was afraid I would not know how to do it. I feared making mistakes and feared making a fool of myself — but there is no need for that. Learning means allowing ourselves to make mistakes; and our subconscious mind can link up each little bit that we gain, until in the end we have surely learned it all.

No matter how long you have thought of yourself as a failure, if you want to change now, you can shape a prototype of success. No matter in what field you want achievement, the basic work you must do is the same — plant the seeds of success, and those seeds will naturally grow into a fine harvest.
Here are some “success” secrets you can use:
I believe the Buddha’s words are wise guidance.
Everything I come into contact with will succeed.
Society holds many opportunities for everyone, myself included.
I have found a new doorway to success.
There are many people who can help me.
I have the ability to accept the Dharma.
The Buddhas and bodhisattvas watch over me.
You can take each of the sentences above and repeat them to yourself whenever you have a free moment, letting these thoughts fill your mind.
You need not worry about “how” to put them into practice; the opportunity will come to you of itself. You have only to trust your inner wisdom and let it guide you. You deserve to succeed.
There are many notions that we must clear up.
For example:
Money is filthy and vile.”
Actually, money that comes by honest means is neither filthy nor vile.
Money is evil.”
Not necessarily. Money used for proper purposes is not evil at all.
I am poor, and that is a good thing.”
If you are poor because you have no choice in the matter, how can it be called a “good thing”? And if you are poor because you are lazy and make no effort to better yourself, that is a disgrace.
All rich people are bad people.”
Many people are born into very wealthy families; many have succeeded in business. What crime have they committed?
I do not want to become an arrogant person just because I have money.”
Why can one not be both wealthy and humble?
I will never have a good job.”
That is a thought that denies your own talents and refuses to make an effort.
I will never earn enough money.”
If others can, you certainly can too.
Money always goes out faster than it comes in.”
That means one does not know how to manage money.
I am always in debt.”
If there are seven inlets and eight outlets, then of course you will always be spending more than you take in. The question is: why not stop up the leaks?
Poor people will always be poor.”
There are many who started with nothing; they are too many to count.
My parents were poor, so I am certain to be poor too.”
Children of poor families need only work hard, and they can all turn poverty into wealth.
An artist must struggle with poverty.”
Having money does not mean being worldly; money and art do not conflict.
Only those who speculate and cheat have money.”
That is only a very small number of people, and what they do is none of your business. Besides, speculation and cheating will in the end be exposed and bring evil consequences.
I will not have money.”
It is not that you will not; it is that you do not want to.
I have no ability to make money.”
If you have no ability, you can cultivate ability.
Never lend money to anyone.”
If you lend it without wanting it back, then you may.
A penny saved is a penny earned.”
If you lose your nourishment and ruin your health in the process, then it is truly not worth it.
I want to save a great deal of money, to guard against mishaps and disasters.”
Giving and accumulating merit are the best protection.
I hate rich people.”
That is a sign of envy.
I can only make money by doing hard labor.”
To be content with one’s lot and to have a spiritual refuge is a good thing; but if one gives way to self-pity and makes no effort to improve, that is another matter.
Above, I have clarified a few old notions. I believe that once everyone has thought them over carefully and understood them, they will no longer accept those useless old ideas.
Every place hopes for economic prosperity, and overall economic prosperity depends entirely on the efforts of individuals.
To deny the usefulness of money is extremely unwise. All the welfare of society depends on money: building bridges and repairing roads, running schools, building temples
which of these can be separated from money? Whether for oneself, for one’s family, or for society, one cannot deny the value of money.

So far as I know, if a person truly wants to possess wealth, he must first be satisfied with himself and love himself. And having money often brings a person freedom, allowing him to do freely what he likes to do; it is not a matter of how much money, but of each person’s lifelong hopes and their expression.

To let the possession of wealth and spiritual cultivation rise together is everyone’s ideal goal. If we do not believe that we can possess wealth, then when opportunity comes we will often simply let it slip away.
Whatever we focus our minds on will increase; so do not focus your mind on your bills. If you focus your mind on your lack and your debts, you will only become more lacking and more in debt.
You should feel glad about what you already have, and then it will increase.

I often bless everything in my life: my home, my furniture, my appliances, my clothes, my means of transport, my work. All my money, my friends, my sight, my touch, my feelings, my sense of taste, my ability to walk upon this wonderful earth — for these things and these abilities I give a blessing every day.
You should affirm that you yourself do not refuse to possess money.
If a friend of yours invites you to his home for a meal, accept gladly and cheerfully, and do not think that you are merely “exchanging” something with him.
If you receive a gift, accept it graciously; and if the gift is of no use to you, you may pass it on to someone else.
You should keep every kind of exchange flowing smoothly. If you smile at people and say a word of thanks, then others will know that you are glad to receive them.
Breaking Free of Poverty
You need a broader space in which to welcome new things. Clean out your refrigerator and your food cupboard; throw away all those odds and ends that have been wrapped in plastic for ages.

Your wardrobe also needs to be properly cleared out: take the things you have not touched in the past six months and move them elsewhere. If among them there are things you have not used in a whole year, then find a way to clear them out; you may even sell them or give them away — it is no loss even to throw them out.

A cluttered wardrobe means you have a cluttered mind; if you are willing to clear out your wardrobe, it shows that you are willing to clear out your mind. As you clean the wardrobe, you might tell yourself: “Whatever needs clearing out, I will clear out.” In this way your spirit will become clear and bright, and your whole body will feel full of energy.
The Buddha teaches people to be diligent and does not like people to be lazy. We must clear out all negative thoughts the way we clear out a wardrobe, so as to make room for positive thoughts.

There was a time when I too was very negative, always thinking that there seemed to be no hope of my ever escaping poverty. When I heard others say that the reason I was poor was entirely due to this belief in my own consciousness, I was once extremely angry. But after many years, I finally came to understand truly that my poverty was indeed entirely my own responsibility alone.
I once believed: “I am worthless,” “I am powerless,” “Money is very hard to come by,” “I have no talent and no ability.” It was these beliefs that sank me into a state of poverty.

When a person holds negative beliefs, they keep him from being active and from pressing forward. So from this moment on, anyone can open his heart to welcome everything good and to improve his life; do believe that you can have your wish fulfilled.
Rise at once and act! Do not sit there sighing any longer.

One thing is very important. As long as we live within our means, we need not worry about money, and all the less should we fear our bills and expenses. Many people pay their bills as painfully as if they were cutting flesh from their own bodies; yet in fact paying money shows that we have the means to pay. Others give you service and give you things first, and only afterward ask you to pay; you have already enjoyed the benefit beforehand, so paying is only natural. For example: you have a house to live in, so of course you should pay the rent; you use electric lights and a telephone, so of course you should pay the electricity and telephone bills. Every time you pay, you get your money’s worth; the more you pay, the more you receive — only if you have nothing at all can you get things for free.

If you pay with a grudging, unwilling attitude, money will find it hard to come to you, because that shows you are unwilling to work and earn. But if you pay with an attitude full of love and gladness, you will open a door to prosperity. You should regard your money as a friend, let it circulate freely, and not maltreat it.

You have security, and it comes not only from your job, your savings in the bank, your investments, your parents, your wife or husband, but also from the right and the blessing you were born with. Many powers in the universe watch over you, and all the more does the compassionate protection of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
I now truly believe that the power that breathes within my body is the very source that supplies all my needs. Worldly affairs are as simple as that.

Remember: there is nothing to worry about. Do not hate or envy others because they have more money than you — that only delays your own good fortune. Nor should you criticize how others spend their money; that is their business, not yours.

Everyone is governed by his own consciousness. What you need to do is tend your own thoughts with care. You should bless others, knowing that the world holds inexhaustible treasures that everyone can obtain.

Are the benefits you give others very few? Do you look down on those who clean toilets? When you are working in your office and see a porter carrying things, do you ignore him completely? Do you care nothing about going into second-hand shops? When you eat in a restaurant, do you always order the cheapest food?

There is a law of demand and supply — demand comes first, and only then does supply follow. When a person needs money, money will come. Even the poorest family will somehow get enough money to buy food and clothing.

One thing is free, and that is a person’s “enterprising spirit.” A person’s enterprising spirit does not need to depend on money, whereas the source of money does need to depend on that spirit. If you have an ideal for your career and your wealth, and can often picture to yourself how you will succeed, then everything you idealize will come into your life.

I once heard a story told by someone from Hong Kong, and it is one hundred percent true. It is about two sisters, both past forty. The younger was long since married, but the elder was still looking for a husband. She had been looking for at least twenty years; from youth to middle age she had always resolved to marry a rich man or else remain unmarried for life. The trouble was that she was not pretty: her skin was dark and she grew fatter and fatter. Yet she never changed her original resolve, and still held confidence and enterprise toward herself.
Her younger sister was anxious for her and asked friends everywhere to introduce her to wealthy men, but not once did it end happily.

One year a wealthy merchant famous in those parts lost his wife, and as there was no one to care for his daughter at home, he was quite eager to find a new wife. The younger sister learned of this; a friend of hers told her, a friend who knew the rich merchant and so knew the matter very clearly.
For this the younger sister treated this friend to meals, once, twice, three times. Each time in the restaurant she earnestly begged the friend to act as matchmaker for her elder sister.

It is no use,” the friend said, shaking his head again and again. “Many people are seeking a match for him; many young and beautiful ladies want to marry him, and he has found none of them to his liking — to say nothing of your sister. To be frank, she simply does not qualify.”

I know my sister does not have the qualifications, but I beg you to help just this once. If you will only arrange for the two of them to meet once, then even if it comes to nothing, I will be grateful to you all my life!”

And so the elder sister met the rich merchant, and to everyone’s surprise he was most pleased with her, and before long they were discussing marriage. The sister who had resolved to marry a rich man at last had her wish fulfilled and became the wife of a merchant worth tens of millions.

The reason was that the rich merchant had no confidence in young and beautiful women; he feared that their eye was on his money and that no one could tell how things would end. But this elder sister was different: she was well suited to him and much like a mother for his daughter, and he was confident that his family would be happy in the years to come.

This story proves that as long as a person has an ideal, when opportunity comes the ideal will be realized. The elder sister in the story succeeded in the end precisely because she could persevere and had confidence in herself.
There really is a goddess of fortune in this world, who often helps people fulfill their ideals.

I often like to stand alone by the sea and imagine how rich the ocean is; what lies stored in the sea is available to everyone, and it depends on what kind of vessel you hold in your hand to carry it away — is it a teaspoon? A paper cup with a hole in it? A glass? A jar? A bucket? A great net? Or a huge pipe connected to this ocean of abundance?

Look in all four directions: however many people stand at this ocean, this sea of abundance, it has endless things to give each one; people need not fight one another for it, and no one could possibly drain the sea dry. Our vessel is our consciousness, and at any time we can exchange it for a larger vessel and reap an abundant harvest from the sea of humanity.

This world is abundant and infinite, but the universe supplies us only with what we want to possess in our consciousness. So if you want to gain more, you must first enrich your own consciousness. A person’s consciousness is like a bank: when you become aware that you have more creative ability, you are making a larger deposit in the bank of consciousness. Meditation, healing, and affirming all things are all deposits in consciousness, and we should form the habit of making a deposit in the bank every day.

When your career has already succeeded and you have a great deal of money, you should know how to use money, enjoy money, and seek out pleasure; and you should give to people and to society. If you do not, then think about it: what is it all for?

Money should be divided into two parts for use. Giving helps others; seeking pleasure helps yourself, making you happy and full of life. If you do neither of the two, then there must be some bad old belief holding you back, and you must find a way to cast out these old beliefs.

Do not cling to money. You must clearly understand that the sole purpose of money is to make others and yourself happy; it has no other use at all. If you never use your money at all, then what can you do? What can you have?

Besides this, we must also eliminate the belief in a “fixed income.” Do not limit yourself; do not assume that you can only have a certain amount of income or wages. Your income or wages are only one channel; they are not the total source. You have a total source, and that is the whole universe.

There can be many channels. We must open ourselves to welcome these channels. We must accept in our consciousness that money can come by many different channels. As long as we develop our own potential well, every one of us has the opportunity and the ability to obtain enough money. Believe that you are a person of unlimited ability, walking on a broad and endless road, about to receive from sources in every direction.

There was a writer who worked very hard to increase her own income, often believing herself to be a writer who could earn more money. One day she was eating dinner in a restaurant, and no sooner had she chosen a seat and sat down than an old man selling lottery tickets came to her table and asked whether she would like to buy one. This woman writer was very compassionate; she simply wanted to make the old man happy and did not want to disappoint him, so she casually drew a ticket and, smiling, bought it. To her surprise, that ticket won a huge prize and brought her a great fortune. Then her newly published work became very popular, sold out completely, and went into second and third printings
and so she earned a great deal of money.
This little story tells us that the woman writer first believed in her consciousness that she would have money, and afterward she truly succeeded.
Everyone should take note of the abundant environment around them, and be able to rejoice in that abundance.
We should not greedily expect others to give us things; we should be able to give things to others, and all the more to give things to ourselves.
We use these things for a time, and then they pass on to other people. Sometimes things are kept within a family, but after several generations they still pass on elsewhere.
Life has a natural rhythm. Material things come to us, and will just as naturally depart; when they depart, it is because they are going on to another, better, new place.

Toward the gifts, the praise, and even the charity of others, we must learn to accept gladly. In my early years my mother taught me that when people give me something, I should smile and say “Thank you.” This teaching has benefited me all my life.
If someone praises you, you can return the praise in the same way; then it is like exchanging gifts with one another, and what passes between you is set in circulation.

Every morning we should welcome the new day with joy. We should be glad that we are alive, that we have good health, that we have friends, and that we have the ability to express and create. Every one of us should manifest the joy and the meaning of being alive.
Every day we should wholeheartedly enjoy life, unfold life, and do good. We should make the journey of life move upward and break free of poverty.
We should listen with love to the instructions our bodies give us.”

Generally speaking, our illnesses are all of our own making. Our bodies are very much like the most wondrous machine in the world: they can reflect our inner thoughts and beliefs, and they often “converse” with us, telling us how things stand with them. We should take some time to listen attentively.

Even in ordinary times, every cell in our body is responding to our every word, our every thought, our every action. A person who forever wears a long face shows that he has neither happiness nor love. The face of an old person clearly reveals the habits of thought of a lifetime, so from an old person’s facial expression we can tell what kind of person he has been.

In this section I will list the mental conditions that create illness, and also tell you how to create health. I am now inquiring into just how we create certain common physical problems, and why these problems arise. Though it is not accurate for every single person, it can give each of us some effective guidance. Ninety to ninety-five percent of patients have been helped by this guidance, and among them were not a few whose condition improved after medicine had failed.

Our “head” symbolizes ourselves. It is with our head that we present ourselves to the world; people know us through knowing our head. If there is some discomfort in our head, it shows that we must have a very large problem.

Hair” symbolizes strength. If we are often tense and afraid, the pores from which the hair grows contract and the hair cannot breathe; when the hair cannot breathe it loses its life and falls out. If this condition is not improved, in time it will make us bald.

Since women began to enter the “business world,” they too, because of tension and depression, have begun to face the problem of baldness. This is very different from the old days of “men outside, women inside.” Women of that era, under lighter pressure, seldom faced the threat of baldness; and even men, since the various competitions of former times were not as fierce as they are now, had far less trouble with baldness.

A person who is constantly tense and under pressure does not show that he is making an especially great effort; it only shows that he is rather fragile. Only one who can relax, be at ease, and yet be focused is truly strong and secure. We should relax our bodies more, and relax our scalps even more, so as to avoid bringing on baldness.
Now we can try letting ourselves relax, and we should practice this relaxation often. After you have practiced for a while, you will find that you are plainly very different from before.

Ears” symbolize our ability to hear. If a person has trouble with his ears, it usually shows that there are certain things he does not want to hear, and even less does he want to hear what others have to say.
If one is not a little deaf and a little dumb, one cannot be the head of a household.” If one grows used to playing deaf and dumb, then in time the ears really do go deaf.

Conversely, if a person’s ears are free of illness and pain, and he can train himself to listen attentively even to the faintest sound, then even if he lives past a hundred his hearing can still remain very good.

Earache is quite common in small children. This is because children are often forced to listen to all kinds of talk from adults, talk they simply do not want to hear. Add to that parents who forbid a child to express anger: the child’s anger is suppressed, and that brings on the earache.

Eyes” symbolize our ability to see. If we have trouble with our eyesight, it usually means we are tired of looking at certain things — perhaps books and newspapers, perhaps things that often appear in our lives, whether they are past, still present, or yet to come. It is we who first have the desire to avoid them; the eyes take the suggestion, and so the power of sight is reduced.

When a small child wears glasses, it may be because he has inherited near-sightedness, or it may be that there are certain circumstances at home he does not want to see. A child has no power to change his family; all he can do is wish that he might not see the things he does not want to see, and so his eyesight weakens under suggestion, to lessen the trouble in his heart.

Many people, because they were willing to clear up and amend the bad things that had happened before they began wearing glasses, also improved their eyesight: their near-sightedness decreased, and some who had worn glasses no longer needed to wear them. This phenomenon truly gives one food for thought.

We might ask ourselves: is there something we do not want to face right now? Or are afraid to face? Afraid to face in the future? If you can deal clearly with yourself, then nothing will happen to you. This is a very useful question, and worth pondering well.

Headache” comes from a confused mind and from seeing oneself as worthless. When one has a headache, one should ask oneself: just what is wrong? Then comfort yourself and encourage yourself, let all the problems be resolved, and the headache will naturally be cured.

People who often suffer from migraines want too much to be perfect and create too much pressure for themselves; at the same time they often suppress themselves and never dare to vent their grievances. Yet whenever they are about to get a migraine, if they can take moderate exercise and recreation, the migraine will stop at once. Relaxation of the mood can dispel tension and pain. Though a person in the grip of a migraine does not feel like seeking recreation, it is truly worth a try; it is absolutely beneficial.
Neck” and “throat” are very wonderful; this region is very complex.

Our neck is very close to the head and very much like a passage for thought. If a person has trouble with his neck, the body is hinting that toward some situation or some point of view he is too stubborn and inflexible.

Virginia Satir was a brilliant family therapist. She once made a very unusual survey and found that people will wash dishes in as many as two hundred and fifty different ways. This fact tells us that if we look from only one angle and not from others, we are in effect shutting out the greater part of the world. If a person’s attitude toward life could be as flexible as his neck, then his neck would hardly ever give him trouble.

The throat has the ability to speak for us, but it is connected with the nose, and when the nose takes in bacteria the throat is affected. Yet bacteria are everywhere; why is it that some people easily have throat problems while others do not? It all depends on whether the person has some psychological trouble. One who feels he has no power to make decisions for himself is sure to have a weak throat.
If a sore throat comes together with a cold, that too is because his confused thinking has weakened his resistance, and so it has come about.

Many people live only for others and can never do what they themselves wish to do; they are forever trying to please their mother, their father, their husband or wife at home, their supervisors, colleagues, and customers at work
Such people are unhappy in spirit and are especially prone to colds and sore throats.
The same is true of problems with the tonsils and the thyroid.

We should pay attention to our own coughing and that of others. A cough is expressing something, or reacting to something; many people’s coughing expresses dissatisfaction with their environment, or even a subconscious wish for others to notice them.

The greatest cause of coughing is resistance — resistance to bacteria, resistance to dust, resistance to everything else. At a very successful concert, hundreds and thousands of people sit in perfect silence, listening quietly; those who had colds and coughs do not cough at such a time either.

Conversely, in certain low-grade theaters, though the audience is only a few dozen or a hundred, there is often a great hubbub, with coughing rising and falling on every side, and not a moment of quiet.

All this shows that coughing is not simply a physical ailment, but something a person can create at any time and stop at any time. When I am teaching and a student coughs, I ask him to stand up and ask whether he disagrees with what I am saying, or whether there is really something wrong with his throat. And most of the students I ask stop coughing right there.
Arms” symbolize our experience of life. They have the ability and the potential to embrace: the upper arm has to do with our potential, the lower arm with our ability.

Our “hands” are often used to grasp, to clutch, to hold. We let things come and go between our five fingers, and sometimes we hold on tight and will not let go. We “set our hand” to helping others do things, and one who does it quickly is called “quick-handed.”

Our hands can be very gentle, or, through excessive thinking, the palms can become hard and the fingers rough. One who keeps his hands tightly clenched shows that he has fear: fear that he will lose something, fear that he will not have enough; and once fear gains the slightest hold, nothing at all remains.

If a person always holds tight to the one he loves and will not let go, that only makes him lose the loved one sooner, for no one appreciates an overly tense person for long. People who grip your hand tightly when shaking hands are usually not open-hearted enough.

One should know that in this life everything is destined, and if one is to strive for anything, one can strive only by doing good. With this realization in one’s thoughts, one naturally opens the heart and no longer clings; and so the hands will naturally no longer show tension. You should know that whatever is truly your own cannot be taken from you by others, so you may set your mind quite at ease.

Fingers” — those who have trouble with their fingers should relax themselves as soon as possible and stop clinging so tenaciously to people and to things. Some people accidentally cut their fingers; this is not purely an accident. Their ego is in an unhappy situation, and their spirit is very unfocused.

Back” is the pillar of our body; a good back also means receiving the support of others, and being full of strength. If we have trouble with our back, it means we feel we are not getting the support we deserve. In fact, besides the support of work, family, husband or wife, and friends, we are in truth also supported by life itself; and one who constantly does good is supported all the more by all the auspicious powers of the universe.

Some people have discomfort in the upper back, perhaps because they feel that their spouse, friends, or employer do not understand them or do not support them, which discourages them and so affects the smooth flow of blood in the upper back, producing pain.

Trouble in the lower back often comes from worrying about not having enough money. Many people take money to be the most important thing in life, thinking that without it they cannot survive. In fact, under normal circumstances a person will not starve to death, freeze to death, or die of poverty, so there is no need at all to worry. With two hands a person can obtain everything, and the light of auspiciousness shines upon every kind-hearted person.

Our “lungs” symbolize our ability to receive and to give life. Problems with the lungs usually mean that we are afraid to receive life, or perhaps feel that we have no right to experience a full life. You should know that a person has life because of good causes planted in past lives; you should trust that you are a good man or a good woman, and not give yourself up as hopeless.

Traditionally, women’s breathing has always been very shallow; they thought themselves too delicate to let themselves breathe deeply. Today all this is changing. Women can hold their own place in society and be full members of it with complete personhood, and so they have begun to breathe deeply and fully. I am very glad to see women taking part in athletic competitions. Women have always worked indoors, and only in modern times have women become as strong and active as men; because of this, their bodies have grown strong.

Emphysema and excessive smoking come from denying one’s own life. Such people hold a stubborn notion that they are not meant to live long, and so they indulge in harmful habits. If a person wants to give up smoking, he must first change this basic belief.

Breasts” symbolize a mother’s love in feeling and in behavior. If we have problems with our breasts, it usually means we feel an excessive “mother love” toward a person, a place, a thing, or an experience.

One of a mother’s duties is to help her child “grow up.” But she must know when to open her hands and stop controlling her children, letting them develop on their own; she should not overprotect them, should not forever prepare everything for them, but should enable them to manage their own life’s journey. Very often, excessive mother love actually weakens the power to nourish.

Cancer of the breast comes from deep resentment and hatred, which affect the functioning of the cells. Buddhism calls “greed, hatred, and delusion” the three poisons, and it is quite right: the toxins of these three poisons are no small matter, and they are the root of many disasters.

Heart” symbolizes love; blood symbolizes joy. A heart full of love can send the blood through our whole body. When we deny joy and love, our heart contracts and loses its elasticity. As a result the blood does not flow smoothly, and anemia and heart disease arise. People with heart disease are not light-hearted, happy people; generally speaking, they are strong at “picking things up” but weak at “putting them down.”

When the Buddha instructed his disciples, he would say “let it go” three times in succession. For one who can let go, his heart disease will be healed accordingly; even if one blood vessel is blocked, a new vessel will grow in its place.

Our “stomach” digests not only food but also our new ideas and life experiences; when there is something wrong with our thoughts and feelings, our stomach will have trouble too. Trouble in the stomach usually means we do not know how to absorb a new experience; we are afraid, and that affects this digestive function.

People who rarely travel by boat often get seasick: their stomach is uncomfortable, they vomit without stopping, and they cannot eat. On the same boat, the passengers are all like this, but the crew who sail the boat are not affected at all. That is because the former fear this experience while the latter have grown used to it and absorbed it, so the stomach’s reaction is different. The same is true of flying, except that there are now medicines to prevent vomiting, so the situation is not quite so obvious.
People with stomach trouble are hard to cure with medicine; only after their mood and their environment have completely changed can their stomach trouble be cured without medicine.

People who recite the Buddha’s name and eat vegetarian food seldom have stomach trouble, mainly because they have a correct outlook on life and are not so full of attachments; thus their digestive systems are better than those of people who do not believe in Buddhism.

Our “legs” carry us forward toward life’s goals. Trouble in the legs usually means we are afraid to move forward, or do not want to move in a certain direction. Varicose veins in the legs mean that one stands in a place of hatred and does hateful work, having lost his joy. If such people conduct themselves according to the Buddha’s instruction, fearing no hardship and accumulating much merit, their leg pain will naturally not recur.

Knees,” like our neck, have to do with our ability to adapt; knee pain indicates pride and stubbornness. When we move forward, we are often afraid to bend, too stiff, afraid of our road, unwilling to accept new guidance. If you have trouble with your knees, you might ask yourself: am I proud, do I refuse to change my life, do I refuse to adapt to a new road? You must cast out stubbornness and resolve to change.

Life is flowing and in motion; if we want to be happy, we must adapt to life and move along with it. A willow tree sways with the wind, and at every moment it is so graceful, so naturally at one with life.
To kneel and bow before the Buddha shows your humility, your inclination toward good, and your lack of stubbornness; it benefits not only your knees but also the future course of your life.

Our “feet” show how strong or weak our faith is. Many old people have trouble walking. On the surface it seems to be the decline of bodily function; in fact, it is the loss of faith, a feeling that they have come to the end of life’s journey and that there is no road or direction left to tread with confidence. Once seated, they do not want to stand up; once standing, they only shuffle slowly and do not want to walk. There are many things they do not want to take part in; they shrink back, wanting to conserve their little remaining energy. This is a mistaken way to behave. Function does not decline because of age, but declines because it is not used — just like a machine: the less you use it, the more it rusts and breaks down.
Small children have no problem with faith, and so their feet are very healthy: they can not only walk but run and jump.

When the American president Eisenhower was a boy he fell ill: his leg was in serious trouble and his high fever would not come down. The doctors repeatedly urged that his leg be amputated in order to save his life and bring the fever down. His parents were at first unwilling for their son to lose his leg, but later they too agreed with the doctors’ proposal, thinking it better than giving up his life.

Eisenhower himself opposed this. He begged his brother to bolt his door and let no one touch his body. He even instructed him that he might burn with a higher fever, high enough to make him unconscious, but that even so he must keep guard and on no account let anyone in to take away his leg.
His brother swore that he would carry out the mission, and he truly did. No matter how family and doctors tried to persuade him, he held to his original resolve.
At last a miracle appeared! In the days that followed, the swelling and pain in the patient’s leg gradually subsided and the fever gradually receded, until in the end he made a complete recovery.
This boy, who later became president of the United States, had faith; though his leg was attacked by germs, his fighting spirit meant that they could not defeat him.

We customarily describe a poor doctor as one who “treats the head for a headache and the foot for a footache,” not knowing how to find the underlying cause in the patient and treat it thoroughly. This view is correct; and if one can further understand that all causes of illness are bound up with a person’s beliefs, then it is all the more correct.
Belief is the chief key to whether one is healthy or not. And all unhealthiness from head to foot can be healed by the person himself, more effectively than by relying on a doctor.

A person’s beliefs depend in turn chiefly on faith. Faith is the chief commander of conduct, like the axle of a clock; the axle directs all the parts in their movement, and only when the axle is steady and sound do the parts move correctly.
The Buddha tells us that worldly affairs have cause and effect; our health and our illness also have cause and effect. The “fruit” is what others can see; the “cause” is clearest only to oneself.

Everyone knows that smoking can cause lung cancer, but smoking is not the true cause. The true cause is: why does a person smoke? Why, knowing that smoking is bad, does he keep on smoking? Why, knowing he ought to quit, does he still not quit?

Here we can see all the more clearly the importance of a person’s faith, the importance of conviction. A person who believes in Buddhism will never smoke; even if he once smoked, he will give it up entirely. One whose convictions are distorted cannot generate strength within himself to bring himself happiness, and so must rely on smoking a few harmful cigarettes to “produce” happiness — what does that amount to?

It is the same with drinking. Drinking harms the liver and can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer, yet one whose convictions are wrong still drinks, making drinking the sole joy of life without regard for the consequences.
Drink is not the true cause of illness, because drink does not run into a person’s mouth by itself. Why does one drink? Why can one not stop drinking? That is the true cause.
A person who believes in Buddhism will never drink.
