Human life is long or short, and the length has its own “cause.” Since in this world there are people who live past a hundred, to a hundred and ten or a hundred and fifteen years, and who yet live healthily and joyfully, this can prove that humans are a temporary union of the four great elements — earth, water, fire, and wind. As long as the four elements are in harmony, one need not be ill, need not die young, need not have a short life.
What others can accomplish, we too should be able to accomplish.
The mistaken convictions and mistaken conduct of the past can still be corrected today — it is not too late.
Practicing according to the Buddha’s instruction: precepts, meditation, and wisdom.
Not only do we live in health, we can also attain nirvāṇa and be liberated from the cycle of birth and death!
Each of us has a story — a true story, one lived through in person. I too have my story. Though the past has become the past, when I recall it, it still stands before my eyes, vivid as if present.

The experiences of a life are the record of our being, and are useful material. This material may serve as a reference for oneself and for others as well. Precisely because my story holds blood and tears, sorrow and despair — and because I endured them all — I am willing to make it public.

The Buddha said: life is good. Indeed, in a life of suffering we have only to follow the Buddha’s instruction, to plant good causes as much as we can, to clear away the bitter fruits, and to summon our willpower and press forward. The road ahead may be winding and hard, but it is better than retreating or standing still. Belief in the Buddha helps the mind and helps the body — the facts are before our eyes to prove it.
May my story give you insight; may the Buddha’s teaching give you guidance.
When I was still a little girl of eighteen months, my parents divorced.

Because of my tender age I did not know how great an effect this had on me, but my mother had to go out to work as a hired hand in another’s household. She sent me to a strange place, to be cared for by strangers. There I cried for three weeks without stopping, so that those caring for me were at a loss and did not know what to do. My mother could only take me home and think of some other way.
As a single parent she raised me, and I came to love and honor her. Yet in the end she could not devote herself wholly to caring for me, and this is what I grieve over deeply.

I never knew the reason my mother married my stepfather. Was it because she loved him, or because she wanted to give her child a happy home? In any case, it was not a wise move. My stepfather had been raised in a traditional German family and had a very brutal nature; in the way he treated us he could not free himself of that brutal habit.
My mother later became pregnant with my younger sister. By the 1930s the world economy was in depression, and our family became an even more brutal and darker home. I was only five years old then.

As the saying goes, misfortunes never come singly. Just when I was five years old, a neighbor of ours, an old drunkard, raped me. I clearly remember the doctor examining me, and I remember that in the courtroom I was the victim. Though the man was punished by the law and sentenced to fifteen years in prison, I was endlessly blamed: “It was all your fault!”
Therefore for many years I worried, fearing that once the man finished his sentence and left prison, he would come to take revenge on me for having put him there.
Most of my childhood I endured physical and sexual abuse. My self-esteem grew lower day by day; nothing had a good effect on me, and I felt that even the outside world was a vicious cycle.

When I was in the fourth grade, one incident can show what my life was like then. Our school held a party and there were many cakes to be given out to the students. Except for me, the children of the school all came from comfortable middle-class families; by contrast my clothing was the shabbiest. I wore a ragged haircut, long black shoes, and the smell of raw garlic in my mouth — a smell that came from my being forced every day to eat raw garlic “to keep away parasites.”

We never had cake at home, because we simply could not afford it. An old woman nearby took pity on me and gave me ten cents every week; and on my birthday she would give me a dollar. But the ten cents were all used for household expenses, and the dollar bought the underwear I wore that year.

That day the school party handed out many cakes. The children who ate cake every day each received two or three pieces; but when the teacher came to me — and of course I was last in line — she gave me not a single piece, because they had all been given to the other classmates.

I was very sad at the time, but now I clearly understand that it was because I then presented myself at school as worthless, undeserving of any reward, that I was placed last in line and could not get even a piece of cake. It was entirely that I made myself disagreeable; they were only reflecting their displeasure with me.

When I was fifteen, my understanding had awakened and I could no longer endure the sexual abuse, so I ran away from school and home. I found a job as a waitress in a restaurant. Although the work was hard, it was far easier than all the physical labor I had done at home. Because I had developed not a shred of self-esteem, I was famished for love and care, to the point that I would give my body to anyone who showed me concern.
Just after my sixteenth birthday, I gave birth to a baby girl.

I felt I had no ability to care for her, so I found her a good, loving home — a couple without children who greatly hoped for a baby. I went to live in their home for four months before giving birth, then went to the hospital to deliver, and the child took their name from birth.

Because circumstances were thus, I could not experience any of the joy of being a mother; instead there was only a sense of loss, along with guilt and shame. Those were days filled to the extreme with shame, and I only wished to get through them as quickly as possible. All I remember of my baby girl is her big toe, which was like mine — quite unusual. If we ever meet again, I think I would recognize her just by seeing her big toe.

When the baby was five days old, I left. I returned home, and my mother no longer wished to endure the abuse of her second husband, so I said to her: “Let us go together. You need not suffer all this any longer; I will take you away from here.”
She came with me, leaving behind my ten-year-old sister, who had always been loved by her father.

I helped my mother find a cleaning job at a small inn and settled her in a place where she could feel free and comfortable. Feeling my duty was done, I went with a girlfriend to Chicago. At first I intended to stay only a month, but in the end I went and stayed thirty years, and never once returned.

In those early days of mine, in my childhood, I experienced much violence; and because I later developed poorly and felt myself worthless, I attracted only men who treated me badly, even beating me. If I had gone through the rest of my life endlessly resenting and blaming men without knowing how to change myself, I might still be just as miserable to this day. But after much positive work and experience, my self-esteem grew, and that kind of bad man at last gradually left my life.

In the past I believed deep in my subconscious that I was only meant to be abused, so even men whose conduct was very bad I still accepted. If my own thinking had not been wrong, I would not have drawn such men to me. Now, any man who abuses women has nothing to do with me. There is no longer any mutual attraction between us.

In Chicago I at first did only menial work. After a few years I went to New York and was fortunate enough to become a high-fashion model. But being a model for those famous fashion designers did not help me gain much self-esteem; rather it gave me all the more chances to find fault with myself, and I refused to admit that I was beautiful.

I kept working in the fashion world. Many years later I married an English gentleman of excellent character and high education. We traveled all over the world, met famous people, and even dined at the White House.
Though I was a fashion model and had married such a good man, my self-esteem was still very low.

After fourteen years of marriage, I had just begun to believe that all that was good could last unchanged, when one day he suddenly announced that he had fallen in love with someone else and was preparing to end our marriage. At that time my suffering truly defies description.

But time passed day by day and I went on living; then I began to feel my life changing. A fortune-teller predicted that in autumn a small thing would happen, and that this small thing could greatly transform my life. I paid no attention to such predictions. A few months later autumn came, and quite by chance I attended a gathering of the “Religious Science Association” held in New York City. Everything was quite unfamiliar to me, yet within me there was a feeling urging me to “listen with care.” I therefore listened with care, and joined the gatherings and study courses they held every Sunday. The Buddhist courses gave me the greatest interest and inspiration.

After this, the world of fashion and adornment gradually lost its hold on my interest; I wondered how many more years I could go on concerning myself with my waistline and the shape of my eyebrows. From an ignoramus who had not finished middle school, I became an eager student, reading book after book on religion and healing. The “Religious Science” center became my new home. Though most of my life went on as before, all this new learning began to take up more and more of my time.
Three years later I was able to apply for special membership in that center. Later I passed the examination and became a study counselor there.
This was only a beginning. After this I became a meditator, and then entered a university.
This university was truly very suitable for me. The first year of study was held every Monday, with subjects such as biology, chemistry, relativity

and the like. Before I had only heard others mention them; now I could study them myself, and I learned with great joy. We took examinations every Saturday morning and had Sundays off, and this was so every week.

The university was in Iowa, which was not so noisy as New York City. After dinner we all returned to our rooms to review our lessons. I was the oldest student in the school, and I loved every minute of my school life. The school forbade smoking, forbade drinking, and all the more forbade drugs; we meditated four times each day.
After graduating I left the school. At the airport, people were smoking everywhere, which made me very uncomfortable.

Back in New York, I began to study the higher courses of “Religious Science.” I was very active there and took part in many activities. Then I began to give lectures and also to meet those who came for help.

I took part in many kinds of work and wrote a small book titled “Heal Your Body.” The book describes the mental states that produce bodily illness. After finishing it I held lectures everywhere and led beginning courses.
Then one day the doctor announced that I had cancer.

My origins were very poor; I had been raped at five and was a child often sexually abused, so it is not hard to understand why I would develop gynecological cancer. Like everyone who learns they have cancer, upon hearing the doctor’s announcement I at once became very frightened and panic-stricken. But because I had already been treating others, and knew that a change in a patient’s mind can indeed cure the illness, I thought this should be the time for me to prove it upon myself.

I knew that the cause of cancer is mostly long-standing anger; this accumulated anger produces toxins that slowly invade the body’s cells, making them lose their normal development, and it then forms into cancer. Because of my childhood circumstances, I had never been able to dissolve my anger and resentment toward “others.” This time I could no longer waste time; I still had much work to do.

Cancer is an “incurable disease,” and those four words are so terrifying to most people; but to me, having calmed down, they made me understand that this disease cannot be treated from outside. The only way to treat it, I thought, was to seek within, to find a cure at the root. If I had surgery, it would only remove the cancer cells; if I did not change the mental system that had created these cancer cells, then the doctors would keep cutting away at my body until there was nothing left to cut. I did not like that approach.

I believed that if on the one hand I had surgery to remove the cancer cells, while on the other I cleaned up the mental system that had led to the cancer, then the cancer would not recur. If cancer or some other illness recurred, I did not believe it was because the doctor had not cut it all out; I believed it was because the patient had not changed his mental state.

I further believed that if I could clean up the mental system of the cancer, then I would not need surgery at all. So I stalled for time with the doctor, telling him that for the moment I had no money to pay the hospital fees, and the doctor agreed to give me a three-month deadline.
I at once set about actively treating myself, seeking out and investigating all methods of healing apart from medicine, while turning my whole heart to the Buddha.

I went to several natural health-food stores and bought all their books on cancer. I also went to the library to read more. I looked into “reflexology” and “colonic therapy.” I felt these would all help me. It seemed I was led by good karma to the right place, and I even met a person who was of great help to me.

This is how it came about: after I read about “reflexology,” I hoped to find such a specialist. I went to attend a lecture. Usually I would sit in the front row to listen; this time, against my custom, I quite naturally sat down in the back row. Within less than a minute, a man arrived and sat down beside me — he proved to be a specialist in “reflexology,” and a professional who made house calls. After talking with him I invited him to my home, three times a week for two consecutive months of massage, which was of great help to me.

I knew I should love myself more than before and value myself more. For in my childhood I had received very little love; no one made me feel happy and content, and so I too had formed the same attitude as theirs, endlessly belittling myself and criticizing myself, until it gradually became my own habit. In Buddhism I came to realize that I should not only love others and encourage myself, but also do many good deeds. Before, I knew that I ought to do this, yet I put it off day after day — just as those who wish to diet keep postponing it one day at a time. Now I could no longer delay.

At first many of the good deeds I had to do seemed difficult to me. But when I resolutely kept on doing them, I found that certain circumstances arising in my life were changing little by little, changing for the better. They no longer discouraged me, and my health made notable progress. I knew I had to keep on, to continue doing good, and to give my whole heart and strength to everything.

Yes, I did indeed have a gray childhood, full of mental, physical, and sexual abuse. But that was many years ago; I should not still be using it now to torment myself. It was precisely because I did not forgive others that cancer cells arose and attacked my body.

With the help of a good Buddhist teacher, I dissolved all the old, hidden anger, gradually coming to the state of loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, which made me feel far more at ease. Then I began to connect, one by one, the stories my parents had told me about their own childhoods. I could clearly see the circumstances of their lives. As my understanding grew, I began to feel compassion for my parents’ suffering; and the blame I held toward them in my heart slowly began to dissolve.

In addition I learned to eat vegetarian and no longer ate meat, the better to help my body clear away the toxins that had accumulated over many years of eating improper food. Besides improper food being able to accumulate and produce toxins, improper thoughts too can accumulate and produce toxins. So I advanced on both fronts: besides eating many green vegetables, I also worked hard at precepts, meditation, and wisdom.

I did not go to the hospital for surgery; I was only actively doing this thorough work of clearing the mind and body. Six months after I was diagnosed with cancer, the doctor gave me confirmation of a result I had long known myself — I had not the slightest trace of cancer!
Because of this firsthand experience, I know all the more that any illness can be cured, so long as we are willing to change our habitual thoughts, beliefs, and conduct!

Some things appear to be tragedies, yet they may turn disaster into blessing and become the best experiences of our lives. It was precisely because I had the experience of cancer that I learned so much more, and thereby gave my life a newer value.

My thinking grew clear, and I knew at last what truly mattered most to me. So I made a decision: to leave New York City, which had no trees and a poor climate. When my patients heard I was leaving, they feared that without me their confidence would greatly diminish. For their sake I planned to go back twice a year to see how they were progressing. Ordinarily we kept in touch by telephone, able to call at any time to discuss everything.
So I wound up my career in New York, took the train at leisure, and went to California, with Los Angeles as my destination, to begin once more to realize my whole plan.

Los Angeles had been my birthplace, my native home, but now I hardly knew anyone there except my mother and younger sister, who lived an hour’s drive away. For my family had never been a family with close ties to people. When I saw my mother again this time, I learned that her eyes had long been blind. My mother had kept this fact hidden, and no one had told me, which suddenly left me shocked and disheartened. My sister was too busy to come and see me, so I had to begin building my new life all alone.

Fortunately, the little book I had published, “Heal Your Body,” was a best-seller and opened many doors for me. When I took part in gatherings, I often introduced myself there and built many relationships. In the first six months I seized the time to go often to the beach to rest my body and mind. I knew that later I would grow busy, and then I would have no time for such leisurely enjoyment.

As the days passed, the patients who came to see me gradually increased. I was also invited to speak in many places; Los Angeles welcomed me, and everything was very successful. A year later I moved into a spacious, comfortable dwelling. Under the Buddha’s protection, everything was so easy and smooth.

My new life in Los Angeles was better beyond measure than the circumstances of my early years, and it taught me that a person’s life can, after a transformation of self, undergo a correspondingly great transformation.

One night my sister called me — the first call in the two years since I had come to Los Angeles. In the call she told me my mother had accidentally broken her spine. My mother was ninety, blind in both eyes, and her ears no longer served her. Once she had been a very strong, independent woman; now, in the twinkling of an eye, she had become such a suffering, helpless old person. Such is the impermanence of life.

My mother’s broken spine, however, dissolved the estrangement between my sister and me, and at last we began to have dealings with one another. I found that my sister also had serious problems; sitting down and walking were both difficult and painful for her. Yet she only suffered in silence, and her husband did not yet know she was ill. Moreover, she had no appetite and did not want to eat, very much like one suffering from anorexia.

After a month in the hospital, my mother was released, and to care for her I brought her to live with me. Though I believed in the Buddha, I did not know how to look after my mother properly. I had work to do and could not stay home to nurse her. With no other recourse, I could only pour out my heart to the Buddha: “O Buddha! Please grant me strength, so that I may both serve my mother well and help others!”

My mother came on a Saturday morning; the next Friday I had to go to San Francisco for four days. I knew I could not leave her alone in the house, yet I could not fail to go. For this reason I could only pray to the Buddha once more: “O Buddha! Please grant me strength to solve this difficulty, and before I leave, find a suitable person to help us.”
On Thursday afternoon the difficulty was indeed resolved. A suitable person “appeared” and moved in to manage the household and care for my mother, so that I had no more worries behind me.

I thanked the Buddha, and with all my heart I am certain: the Buddha is an undying lamp, ever lighting the way for those who need its light. From then on I devoted myself wholeheartedly to doing good, and toward my patients and my work I held the spirit of giving, going at it with all my might.
When I was a child, my mother, because of the circumstances, could not protect me well; but now I have the ability to care for her well, and I feel very happy.

My sister had never been close to me, yet now she asked me for a great deal of help; this was another challenge, testing my compassion. Looking back, when I rescued my mother from the firing pit of my stepfather, because he doted on his own daughter from that marriage we had not taken her away as well. I never imagined the stepfather’s perverse temper would carry him so far as to vent the anger and suffering of his failures upon my sister, subjecting her to abuse she had never before known.

My sister’s physical problems came from the great fear and tension of her childhood; these tensions and fears later only increased, never easing. Her husband gave her not a shred of security, so I had to do my utmost to give her a safe environment, and within it seek out a way to heal her.

After my mother came to live with me, things went very well. She exercised four times a day to the best of her ability, and her body grew stronger. I fitted her with a hearing aid so that her ears could hear, and life became more interesting for her. I persuaded her to go to the hospital to have her cataracts removed, and she slowly recovered her sight. Now she can see everything again and is overjoyed; she can pick up books and newspapers to read, which makes her happier still, and we are all delighted for her.

My mother and I, in a way we had never known before, sat down together and talked at length. Between us there arose a new understanding, and we were more at ease with one another; sometimes we even embraced.

My work continued to grow, the staff increased, and a new center was built — no small establishment, with places where students could stay. I am the director of the center, a healer, and a teacher. My heart is very peaceful, and I will continue to do good for the remainder of my life and never stop.
